item.title: [Heavy.com] Red Sox Warned About Adley Rutschman Situation by Veteran Scout
item.dc:creator: Dan Morrison

item.content:encoded:
When the Trade Deadline was approaching, Boston Red Sox CBO Craig Breslow sniffed out a chance to fill a couple of roster holes. That included a major splash move, by trading with the Baltimore Orioles for three-time All-Star and 2023 Silver Slugger at catcher, Adley Rutschman.
It wasn’t a cheap move either. The Red Sox sent a haul back to Baltimore, including catcher Carlos Narvaez, Red Sox No. 2 prospect Anthony Eyanson, MLB Pipeline No. 4 organizational prospect Kyson Witherspoon, and two other minor league players. So, it’s safe to say much was expected of Rutschman.
However, Rutschman wasn’t actually able to deliver much. From the moment he was traded to Boston, Rutschman battled injuries. That ended up hurting him offensively, and he hit just .222 with a .688 OPS in 32 regular season games with the Red Sox. He’d go 1-for-8 in the postseason.
The Boston Red Sox Are Being Warned About Adley Rutschman and His Contract
Because the Red Sox gave up a haul for Adley Rutschman, the feeling was that he wasn’t going to be a rental player. However, he’s not on a long-term deal, which means he very well could end up being a rental player if the Red Sox aren’t careful.
For now, Rutschman remains under team control for 2027. After that, he’s currently set to hit free agency.
However, as one veteran scout said, per MassLive, because of what they gave up, they’ll have to extend. It’s not a matter of a choice anymore, because of what they ended up giving up. That’s whether they actually want to or not.
“I think they painted themselves into a corner with what they gave up,” the scout said. “They have to extend him.”
The reality for the Red Sox and Rutschman is that injuries are an issue. For two years in a row now, he’s failed to play in at least 100 regular season games. That’s not one issue that keeps popping up, either, but a long string of issues. In 2024, it was a hand. In 2025, it was both obliques. Then, in 2026, it was ankle inflammation, a concussion, and wrist inflammation that forced IL stints. He’d later play through a hyperextended elbow.
On top of that, Rutschman has seen his stats decline as he’s battled those injuries. He hasn’t had an OPS above .800 since 2023. That was also the last season he had more than 20 home runs or more than 30 doubles.
Red Sox CBO Craig Breslow on Adley Rutschman
Craig Breslow addressed what the Red Sox think of Adley Rutschman at the team’s end-of-season press conference. That is, that he’s a good player who fits a need. However, he didn’t want to discuss any potential contract extension.
“When we acquired Adley, we did so because he was a really good player at a position of need,” Breslow said. “We felt like he could add to our 2026 outlook. Obviously, he’s under control for 2027, which is great. Beyond that, it’s best just to keep conversations between Adley and me.”
The Red Sox have had issues at the catcher position in recent years. Carlos Narvaez, who was traded for Rutschman, had flashed talent in 2025 as a rookie but had also had major regression since then. Prior to him, there was little to no offense coming from Connor Wong, Christian Vasquez, Sandy Leon, Blake Swihart, A.J. Pierzynski, and more.
In fact, arguably the last great offensive season from a Red Sox catcher was in 2013, when Jarrod Saltalamacchia had an .804 OPS. The last Red Sox player to make the All-Star team was Victor Martinez in 2010. The hope is that Rutschman will change that.
“What I would say is that Adley stepped in as our primary catcher in the middle of the season — which is not easy to do, especially when pitching is a strength of our team — and immediately endeared himself to the pitching staff, the coaching staff and the clubhouse,” Breslow said. “Just a really high-quality teammate and leader.”
For all of MLB, the future of contracts remains up in the air. The CBA negotiations hang over everything. It’s just another factor that everyone needs to consider before making a final decision on extensions.

item.title: [Chowder and Champions] Red Sox' Adley Rutschman trade could become a disaster
item.dc:creator: Elie Deglaoui

item.content:encoded:
I absolutely, 100% understand why the Boston Red Sox traded for Adley Rutschman at the trade deadline, even if they did give up a lot to get him.
It was a big risk. The Red Sox gave up some incredible prospects (Anthony Eyanson, Kyson Witherspoon, Enddy Azocar, and Harold Rivas) to get Rutschman; they traded with the Baltimore Orioles, a division rival; and he is set to be a free agent after the 2027 season.
At the same time, the Red Sox: 1) were in legitimate title contention at the time and were in the midst of their magical late-June-into-early-August streak (the trade deadline was on Aug. 3), 2) desperately needed a catcher if they wanted to compete -- Carlos Narvaez, Connor Wong, and Mickey Gasper (we thought) weren't going to cut it, and 3) didn't have a single better option at catcher either within the organization or on the market. He was an All-Star just this season.
The Rutschman trade has mostly been a disaster for the Red Sox so far. But given how much they gave up for him, they have no choice but to sign him to a potentially monstrous deal, and there is a real chance this entire move comes back to bite Boston.
Adley Rutschman left a lot to be desired with the Red Sox
I understand that Rutschman had dealt with injuries for pretty much his entire time in Boston (he was on the IL due to left wrist inflammation when the trade happened, and he dealt with a right elbow injury for parts of August and September), but that doesn't fully excuse how bad he looked.
In 32 games with the Red Sox this season, the Oregon native batted .222 with five home runs and 13 RBIs. And in the Wild Card series against the New York Yankees, he went 1-for-8 (.125) and struck out three times.
Rutschman did show some flashes, but he never found his groove at the plate. Maybe a full offseason in Boston can help, but it was still incredibly disappointing, seeing how bad he looked after the trade. And given that the Red Sox basically have to sign him to a new deal (on top of all the prospects they gave up, there is still objectively not a better option behind the plate for them), Rutschman's struggles put them in a tough spot.
The next time we see Rutschman, he's going to be 29 years old (maybe even 30, depending on what happens with the lockout). He is in the middle of his peak right now. I still have hope that he's going to turn things around and that this was just a slump and that a full offseason in Boston should help (let's also not act like virtually everyone in the Red Sox' lineup struggled after the trade deadline), but there's no denying that the early returns aren't great, and it looks like there is a world where the risk doesn't pay off in the end.
If Rutschman's struggles continue, this trade could become another big mistake by the Red Sox' front office.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] The Red Sox didn’t upgrade their home run power last offseason. Can they this year? - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Alex Speier

item.content:encoded:
Craig Breslow surveyed the playoff field and reached an obvious conclusion about a path for improving the Red Sox.
“It would be fair to look at some of those other teams to say that they hit the ball out of the park a little bit more than we do,” said the Sox’ chief baseball officer. “It doesn’t really matter how you score, but in the postseason, a lot of runs come via the home run because the pitching is so dominant. So I think that’s a consideration.”
The assessment certainly would have been appropriate at the Red Sox’ end-of-year news conference at Fenway Park on Monday, five days after the team got bounced from the playoffs in two games by the Yankees while managing a total of two runs. But Breslow’s observation was actually offered one year earlier, in the days after the Sox were knocked out of the 2025 Wild Card Series by the Yankees.
Despite identifying power as a priority entering last offseason, the Red Sox lineup took a step backward. In 2025, the Sox hit 186 homers (15th in MLB), had a .324 on-base percentage (eighth), and a .421 slugging percentage (ninth). This year, the Red Sox hit 163 homers (26th), had a .319 OBP (12th), and slugged .398 (20th).
Caveats are in order. The loss of Trevor Story and Roman Anthony for the majority of the year removed two batters capable of driving the ball out of the park. One of the players brought in to offset their absences, Curtis Mead, made just two plate appearances following a July trade with the Nationals before suffering a broken wrist when getting hit by a pitch.
Even with those losses, the Sox’ power deficiency was subject to exaggeration. Fenway Park played as a graveyard for power for much of the year. On the road, the Sox hit 87 homers — tied for 21st in the big leagues and well ahead of the bottom-ranked team in that category, the best-in-baseball Brewers (63). From July 1, the Sox ranked roughly in the middle of the pack in slugging and homers per game.
Still, the Sox didn’t have the depth of power to reliably outslug opponents — especially against playoff-caliber power pitching. The team went deep just 26 times against 95-plus-mile-per-hour pitches, tied for fourth fewest in the big leagues.
On Monday, Breslow — while identifying strengths in the rotation and bullpen, as well as infield and outfield defense — didn’t pretend otherwise.
“Our offense was inconsistent,” Breslow said. “We got on base at a decent clip, but we didn’t really slug. We didn’t hit a ton of home runs. I’m not sure that we took advantage of the unique venue that that we play in. Naturally, we’re going to spend some time thinking about how we improve our offense, and particularly how we build a roster that can thrive at Fenway Park.”
The quick ejection from the postseason — when the Sox allowed four homers to the Yankees, while hitting just two — further reinforced the point, and underscored the biggest lever to pull as the team looks to build a club capable of competing deeper into the playoffs.
“When you get beat in the lopsided manner that we did [in the playoffs], I think we have to evaluate, how do we improve our offense? How do we particularly improve our offense against elite pitching?” Breslow said. “We’re very familiar with our offensive production against pitchers that throw 95-plus and 97-plus (m.p.h.), and I think there are ways to train that. I also think that we have to be aware of roster construction and making sure that we have a resilient offense.”
Beyond the team’s efforts to help develop more power among returning players (while also contemplating the potential impact of Franklin Arias, whose developmental jump has evaluators forecasting him as a potential 15-20 homer hitter), the task of upgrading the offense is different than a year ago.
After the 2025 season, the free agent market featured several top- or middle-of-the-order threats, notably Alex Bregman, Pete Alonso, and Kyle Schwarber. The Sox did trade for a lineup centerpiece in Willson Contreras, but didn’t manage to add a second slugger (with Bregman the most notable near miss).
This year’s free agent class is thinner, with righthanded hitting outfielders Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki, longtime Sox tormenter Brandon Lowe (a lefthanded hitting second baseman), and Nippon Pro Baseball star Teruaki Sato (expected to be posted this offseason) the best power bats on the market.
Those modest options likely explain why the Sox were so aggressive leading up to the trade deadline, not only trading for Mead and Adley Rutschman but making unsuccessful pushes for shortstops Otto Lopez of the Marlins (.396 average against 95-plus-m.p.h. pitches, best among hitters who saw at least 250 such pitches) and Zach Neto of the Angels (.489 slugging against 95-plus, 40th in MLB).
The extent of the midyear effort to upgrade the lineup served as a tell about the team’s offseason focus. There’s little question that power — particularly righthanded pull hitters who can handle velocity with a chance to mash at Fenway — once again offers the biggest potential upgrade. Breslow and the Sox now have an offseason to show whether they can achieve it.
Alex Speier can be reached at alex.speier@globe.com. Follow him @alexspeier.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox' Craig Breslow eyes offensive upgrades for 2nd straight winter
item.dc:creator: Sean McAdam

item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — The Red Sox' 2026 season was strikingly similar to that of the 2025 season. For the second straight season, the team finished third in its division, accumulated a win total in the upper 80s, and got eliminated by the New York Yankees in the wild card round.
So maybe it shouldn't be much of a surprise that the team's chief baseball officer, Craig Breslow, identified the same offseason priority as (almost exactly) a year ago.
"We're in the initial stages of evaluating the season and thinking about our approach to 2027," said Breslow, "but it's not hard to look at the composition of our roster and recognize our starting pitching was consistently very good. I think by a handful of metrics, I think we had the best bullpen in baseball and the best outfield defense in baseball and an infield defense that showed marked improvement relative to the last few years.
"Our offense was inconsistent. We got on base at a decent clip but we didn't really slug (.398, 20th in MLB), didn't hit a ton of home runs (163, 26th) and I'm not sure that we took advantage of the unique venue that we play in. So naturally, we're going to spend some time thinking about how we can improve our offense, particularly how we build a roster that can thrive at Fenway Park."
Indeed, the Red Sox were just 18th in runs scored at home this past season.
Breslow expressed hope that the Sox could see significant jumps in the power department from a number of players just now entering their prime — Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu and Caleb Durbin included – while anticipating a full season from Curtis Mead, who was sidelined for more than two months after being injured in his second at-bat with the Sox.
"And also we're going to have to look at what may be available that's not currently on the roster," Breslow said, "and figure out if there's an opportunity down that path as well."
Breslow said much of the same thing after last season, while making the observation that home runs were the quickest and most efficient way to score runs, and noting that home runs become even more valuable in the postseason. A year ago, teams out-homering opponents were 30-5 in the postseason, and the same pattern is already evident this fall.
The Sox acquired their one major offensive upgrade last winter by trading for first baseman Willson Contreras, and that move paid off handsomely. Contreras enjoyed the best year of his career, leading the team in homers, RBI and OPS. He also hit one of two homers the team managed in its brief postseason.
But clearly, more is now needed.
"There are a lot of reasons to believe the existing offense should be better in 2027," said Breslow. "But we're also going to do everything we can to improve beyond that."
The problem, in part, is that the free agent market is a relatively thin one when it comes to run producers. Last year, Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso headed the free agent class; this year, the two best offensive players appear to be Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki, neither of whom has that kind of power ceiling.
Another issue: should the Sox acquire another bat, where does that fit into the lineup? The team is currently set at catcher (Adley Rutschman), first (Contreras), second (Mead), shortstop (Trevor Story), third base (Durbin) and the outfield is deep with Rafaela, Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran. There could be a DH opening, but it's possible either Anthony or Duran could fill that.
"It can be a bit of a challenge when you kind of go around (the field) and say, 'We think this player is very good, this player is very good and this player is very good,'" said Breslow, "and we think that there's another step forward for them to take. Sometimes that improvement comes from taking a good player and turning them into a great player. That can be internal development or adding players to the organization who are currently out here right now."
This offseason will offer plenty of variables, not the least of which is the looming Dec. 1 lockout and the uncertainty surrounding what a new collective bargaining agreement might bring.
That could mean a busy November as teams rush to get trades or signings done before the sport closes down – or that same flurry might be postponed until a new CBA is agreed upon.
One thing, however, remains clear: the Red Sox, as currently constituted, aren't good enough offensively. And unless they want a third straight winter in which they pursue improvements, that has to be addressed.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox's Wilyer Abreu Gets Shocking Bargain $4.6 Million Contract Update
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have turned their eyes to the offseason.
It’s earlier than they would’ve liked, but they were swept out of the AL Wild Card Series by the New York Yankees, and so now they’ve got to think about what the 2027 campaign will look like.
There’s one area where the Red Sox have the potential to be particularly busy in the offseason — whenever it can begin in earnest after a potential lockout — and that’s salary arbitration.
They’ll have a whopping 17 players up for salary arbitration, if they choose to tender them contracts.
One of the biggest names on that list is Wilyer Abreu, and MLB Trade Rumors writer Matt Swartz has projected values for all the Boston arbitration eligible players.
For Abreu, the number comes out to be quite the bargain.
Wilyer Abreu Contract Projection
The MLBTR projection for Abreu’s salary for the 2027 season comes in at $4.6 million.
For a player with the power, glove and throwing arm of Abreu, it certainly seems like a massive bargain.
That doesn’t consider everything that goes into arbitration, though.
Each player that reaches the major leagues via the minor leagues has six years of club control once they reach the majors.
The first three years have a salary based on the collective bargaining agreement, and they’re considered the pre-arbitration years.
Years four through six of a player’s time with a team are the arbitration years. In each of those offseasons, a player is eligible to go to salary arbitration to determine what he’s paid the following season.
The arbitration process features the team submitting a value and the player submitting one, and the independent arbitrator comes to a conclusion on which one wins out.
Teams and players these days often negotiate in advance to avoid actually going to what can be a contentious hearing, but the value they come out with will still end up close to what it would’ve been in arbitration.
All that said, it matters which year a player is in for the sequence — and this is only Abreu’s first arbitration year. Generally, the first arbitration year comes with the lowest salaries, and they rise in each of the two subsequent years, even if the player is viewed as having exactly the same value each season.
So for Abreu, no matter what he did this season, he wasn’t going to end up with a giant arbitration value.
The Red Sox could always look to give him a higher-paying contract extension and buy out some of his eventual free agent years, but for now, Abreu is headed for arbitration.
Other Red Sox in Arbitration
The list of 17 Red Sox heading to salary arbitration is long.
The full list is: Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, Adley Rutschman, Jarren Duran, Eli White, Kutter Crawford, Connor Wong, Romy Gonzalez, Triston Casas, Andruw Monasterio, Zack Kelly, Greg Weissert, Wilyer Abreu, Erik Miller, Justin Slaten, Jahmai Jones and Tyron Guerrero.
If a team chooses not to tender a player a contract, they instead go right to free agency.

item.title: [Over the Monster] Craig Breslow started building the 2027 Red Sox in 2026
item.dc:creator: Mike Carlucci

item.content:encoded:
The Wild Card series against the Yankees was probably the worst way for the 2026 season to end. Everything that was a problem at any point - struggles to score runs, the bullpen, injuries - all happened at the same time and within a matter of minutes. Two games in a row ended the Red Sox season. This wasn’t the plan. As all the Sox players returned from the WBC to Fort Myers, many riding hot streaks, this looked like a team ready to rocket. Yes, there were questions entering the season. But there were answers that hadn’t been fully formed yet.
After the 2025 season, the Sox were desperate for infield help. Trevor Story, not a guarantee of health or success himself, since arriving in Boston, was coming off a tremendous year, his best for the Red Sox. The rest of the infield was a question mark. Third base was more-or-less vacant after Alex Bregman opted out. Second base was going to be a battle with the future potential of Marcelo Mayer as a leading contestant. First base? Triston Casas? Maybe? Catcher, using the more generous definition of infield, was a tandem based on Carlos Narváez hitting in 2025 and Connor Wong, who couldn’t hit at all. There were at least two guys, which was more than could be said about first base.
Craig Breslow looked at the free agent market. He looked at the trade market. He looked at his own farm system. And in two phases he built the roster that he would live or die with.
We know about phase one. Caleb Durbin was acquired from the Milwaukee Brewers. Willson Contreras was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals. Isaiah Kiner-Falefa was signed to platoon (kinda) with Mayer.
On the free agent market, the Red Sox went in the opposite direction. The promise/hope was two bats. And they passed on Pete Alonso, Alex Bregman, Bo Bichette etc. Aside from Contreras there were no big bats.
What Durbin would share with Willson, besides become Mini Bowser to his Bowser, was control. Contreras was guaranteed to be in town through 2027 with an option for 2028. Durbin will not hit free agency until the 2030s. The same with Mayer. Ranger Suarez, on the other side of the ball, also was signed long-term.
As it would turn out Willson Contreras would not even sniff competition from Triston Casas, who would face a series of injuries that would cost him the season. Not that anyone was worried about having too many first basemen. Caleb Durbin would start off slow with the bat, glacial even, but provide solid defense. He’d go on to set a new career high in home runs while, likely, competing for a Gold Glove.
Marcelo Mayer would underperform and then get hurt. Carlos Narváez would revert to his reputation as a bat-second player. While Connor Wong would provide some offense in a bounce-back season, the catcher tandem as a whole was underwater.
Phase two would be at the deadline. With Durbin rounding into form as The Durbinator, Breslow and his team set their sights on second base and catcher. Turning Connelly Early into Curtis Mead gave them another second baseman with control for years to come. And while the sample size is small, Mead hit 17 home runs in just 87 games. Adding a 30-homer threat to second base would be a tremendous pillar of the offense. Mayer would be traded separately, Mead would get hurt, but the plan was in place.
Similarly, the massive all-in prospect trade for Adley Rutschman was for 2026 and 2027. Connor Wong isn’t a free agent until after the 2028 season so catcher is set for another year and they have time to evaluate Rutschman or find a replacement before 2028. For Breslow’s plan through this summer, when he didn’t know he’d be extended, that’s all that mattered. Build then best team for what could be his last season if they struggled.
Entering 2027 the Red Sox have two catchers. They have an entire starting infield, plus top prospect Franklin Arias. They have Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Wilyer Abreu (plus control of Jarren Duran, and Masataka Yoshida, and Kristian Campbell) in the outfield.
The rotation has Payton Tolle, Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, and Jake Bennett. Boston holds an option on Sonny Gray that he can opt out of, but potentially the entire rotation is headed back for 2027. Starters 6-10 might be a concern, but for a healthy Opening Day major league roster, Breslow took care of that already.
We never actually got to see this team assembled together in 2026. Even if Curtis Mead came into the last game of the season while Garrett Crochet was on the mound, Roman was out. This year, unless there is a big trade to accommodate a move, the Hot Stove season won’t be the same. The roster is basically set. Did Breslow see the lockout as an obstacle? Maybe! He might have been thinking that teams would scramble to make moves before and after and he’d be set. For a team that was seeing it’s window open in 2025, it seems too intentional to put together the whole thing one year in with really only the Story to Arias transition as a big roster move to facilitate.
The performance of the team in 2026 was up and down, but overall we saw a number of good years from this group - Tolle, Abreu, Contreras, Rafaela, and Durbin all provide reasons to be optimistic. Roman Anthony had a good run around the hand injury. Six months off sure would be nice to let that heal. There’s reason to think 2027 can be fun. Maybe distributed a little better too.
Your Opening Day 2027 Boston Red Sox:
C: Rutschman, Wong
1: Contreras
2B: Mead, Sogard
SS: Story, Arias
3B: Durbin
OF: Roman, Rafaela, Abreau, Duran (if he’s not moved/non-tenderd), Campbell
DH: Yoshida

item.title: [puckettspond.com] Twins fan favorite Doug Mientkiewicz takes shots at Willson Contreras, Red Sox after early exit

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox were completely embarrassed by the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series this week. The Yankees swept the Red Sox in two games, winning 9-0 on Tuesday and 9-2 on Wednesday. Boston is now eliminated from the postseason, while New York will play the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series.
With two outs in the bottom of the second inning in Wednesday's game, Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. hit a ball up the middle that Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story smothered on a nice diving play. There appeared to be a play at first base, but Contreras wasn't covering the bag, allowing Chisholm to reach. Luckily for the Red Sox, Contreras' misplay didn't come back to haunt him.
It's one thing for a player to make a defensive mistake once in a game. It's a whole other story if the player makes two defensive gaffes. That's exactly what Contreras did.
Red Sox's Willson Contreras makes defensive mistakes in Wild Card Game 2 loss to Yankees
Boston left-hander Garrett Crochet entered the game in the bottom of the sixth inning with the Yankees leading 2-1. Crochet got the first batter he faced, Spencer Jones, to strike out swinging. However, Jones swung at a ball in the dirt that got away from catcher Adley Rutschman, who was notably slow to retrieve the ball and throw it to first base, allowing Jones to reach first despite striking out.
Contreras was covering first base, but he was positioned on the back of the bag. It wasn't completely Contreras' fault that Jones reached first, but if he had his foot on the front of the bag and stretched to catch the ball, Jones likely would have been out.
Jones stole second base and reached third on a throwing error from Rutschman. He scored on an RBI single from George Lombard Jr. The Yankees scored five more runs in the inning, increasing their lead to 8-1.
It's worth noting that Contreras did his job at the plate Wednesday, going 2-for-2 with a home run and two walks. Unfortunately, his defensive gaffes are what's gaining more attention after Boston's rough loss.
After the loss, Contreras essentially told the media that he believes the Red Sox rely too much on data. Notably, the Red Sox pulled right-hander Sonny Gray from Wednesday's game after he allowed two runs on just 70 pitches over 4 2/3 innings.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said. "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff I would like to say, but I'll state it like that."
Former Twins fan favorite Doug Mientkiewicz, a member of the Red Sox's 2004 World Series team, took a shot at Contreras and the Red Sox after the Boston first baseman's comments.
"How about cover first- or maybe one of your 15 coaches should say something," Mientkiewicz wrote on X. "Oh but they will shoot balls out of a tiny machine on a slab of turf though during pregame. Embarrassing."
Mientkiewicz played for the Twins from 1998-2004. The Twins traded the first baseman to the Red Sox at the 2004 trade deadline.
During his seven years with the Twins, Mientkiewicz hit .275/.367/.408 with 43 home runs and 266 RBI. After his stint with Boston in 2004, Mientkiewicz played for the New York Mets, Kansas City Royals, New York Yankees, Pittsburgh Pirates and Los Angeles Dodgers. He retired after the 2009 season.

item.title: [sportingnews.com] MLB insider reveals Orioles' 'steep' asking price from Yankees for Adley Rutschman | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Conor Liguori
item.description: The New York Yankees targeted several catchers at the trade deadline. Ultimately, they did not acquire a right-handed hitter to platoon with Austin Wells, who received trade interest from another AL East team. On Wednesday, the New York Post's Jon Heyman reported that the Baltimore Orioles inquired about Wells and a few other Yankees players in a potential deal for catcher Adley Rutschman. "The Orioles had a request to the Yankees on the table for star catcher Adley Rutschman at the deadline: pi
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees targeted several catchers at the trade deadline.
Ultimately, they did not acquire a right-handed hitter to platoon with Austin Wells, who received trade interest from another AL East team.
On Wednesday, the New York Post's Jon Heyman reported that the Baltimore Orioles inquired about Wells and a few other Yankees players in a potential deal for catcher Adley Rutschman.
"The Orioles had a request to the Yankees on the table for star catcher Adley Rutschman at the deadline: pitching prospect Elmer Rodriguez, catcher Austin Wells, outfield prospect Yostin Pena plus one of two young starters - either Will Warren or Ryan Weathers," Heyman wrote.
That would have been quite the price for the Yankees to pay for a year and a half of Rutschman, who has dealt with injuries in recent seasons.
The Yankees value Wells' pitching-calling abilities and his work with their pitching staff.
Warren and Weathers could be key contributors to New York's bullpen in the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays. Both pitchers are under team control through at least 2028 (Weathers).
Plus, Rodriguez is an intriguing arm, and Pena hit .323 with six home runs in 23 games at Single-A Tampa.
Did the Yankees need Rutschman that badly? As it turns out, not really.
Wells caught fire at the plate during the later months of the regular season and has continued that trend into the postseason.
For now, Ali Sanchez is a perfectly competent backup.
The Yankees can readdress their catching situation in the offseason.
Not trading four players for Rutschman, who posted a .688 OPS in 32 games with the Boston Red Sox, seems like the correct decision.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox Trade Plans for Jarren Duran Revealed

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox and Jarren Duran have been involved in swirling trade rumors for a while now.
Essentially all of last offseason was spent with the premise that the Red Sox had too many outfielders and that one was bound to get traded.
That never came to fruition, though, and so Duran remained in Boston for the 2026 season.
He struggled mightily, batting just .207 with limited power, and so questions will arise again.
The Red Sox still have the same amount of outfielders. Duran might not be worth as much, but he also might not be as crucial for Boston to keep around.
A year later, could a trade materialize?
That’s one question being asked as the Red Sox enter their offseason after being swept in two games in the AL Wild Card Series by the rival New York Yankees.
There are big questions for the sport of baseball to answer as a whole this winter. In Boston, though, Duran is going to be one of the biggest things to solve, one way or another.
Jarren Duran Trade Plans
ESPN’s David Schoenfield wrote about this question almost immediately following the Red Sox season ending, and he seems to arrive at the conclusion that a trade could definitely be coming.
“That leaves trading Duran on the agenda,” Schoenfield writes. “Roman Anthony’s nearly four-month stint on the IL meant the four-outfielders-for-three-positions problem never actually turned into a problem, but after hitting just .207/.266/.361, Duran is clearly fourth on the depth chart. His trade value took a nosedive, but he still somehow has two years left of team control, and the Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.”
There is certainly value for an acquiring team in the fact that Duran still has two more years under contract. Especially considering what a shortened season might do to player value, a team knowing it would also have Duran for 2028 could be appealing to anyone who still believes in his talent.
There may not be a lot of suitors, but Schoenfield writes that the “Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.” It’ll just be up to Boston at that point to follow through on the deal.
Why Red Sox Offseason Might Be Slow Otherwise
Aside from Duran, Schoenfield doesn’t think Boston will be very busy. They’ve already taken care of a bunch of things.
“While the Red Sox had a revolving door at shortstop and second base in 2026 — six different players started at short and seven at second — those positions will probably be resolved in 2027 with top prospect Franklin Arias and Curtis Mead, the trade deadline acquisition the Red Sox were going to play at second base until he got injured his first game with the team,” Schoenfield writes. “Trevor Story still has one more year left on his contract, but there’s no reason he should be playing ahead of Arias next season.”
Schoenfield also references the recent trades for Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Erik Miller as limiting the need for moves, since those guys all are under contract still.
His only other question: Does Sonny Gray retire, or return, or neither? The Red Sox still have things to figure out, just maybe not as much as some years.

item.title: [Sportsnaut] Red Sox Paid a Massive Price for Adley Rutschman to Win in October. Then They Went 0-2
item.dc:creator: Gary Adornato
item.description: Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October. Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman. They didn’t need him to save their season. They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention. And they certainly didn’t surrender four prospects and their starting major-league catcher simply to hang
item.content:encoded:
Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October.
Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman.
They didn’t need him to save their season.
They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention.
And they certainly didn’t surrender four prospects and their starting major-league catcher simply to hang a Wild Card banner.
Boston was already one of baseball’s hottest teams when it acquired Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles at the Aug. 3 trade deadline. The Red Sox had transformed their season with a remarkable summer surge and were firmly positioned to reach the postseason.
Rutschman was supposed to provide something more.
October.
The Red Sox paid an enormous price to a division rival because they believed adding a three-time All-Star catcher could help turn a playoff team into a championship team.
Instead, their postseason lasted two games.
The New York Yankees completed an embarrassing two-game sweep Wednesday night, beating Boston 9-2 after a 9-0 demolition in Game 1.
Final aggregate score: Yankees 18, Red Sox 2.
Boston managed only seven hits in 18 innings and batted .117 in the series. The Yankees did all of it without three-time American League MVP Aaron Judge, who was sidelined by a calf injury.
And Rutschman?
The expensive deadline addition Boston acquired specifically to make a difference at this time of year couldn’t make one.
Making matters considerably worse, the Yankees reportedly had their own opportunity to acquire Rutschman.
They decided Baltimore’s price was too high.
Then they sent Boston home.
Boston Didn’t Need Adley Rutschman to Reach the Playoffs
This is the most important context when evaluating the trade.
The Red Sox weren’t desperately chasing the final Wild Card position when chief baseball officer Craig Breslow made the deal.
Boston had gone 23-3 beginning July 2, establishing itself as one of baseball’s hottest teams and putting itself firmly on a postseason trajectory before Rutschman ever put on a Red Sox uniform.
That’s why simply pointing out that Boston reached the postseason after acquiring him misses the point.
Reaching October wasn’t supposed to justify the trade.
Winning in October was.
The Red Sox ultimately finished 87-75 and secured a Wild Card berth. Then the Yankees eliminated them in two games.
So what exactly did Boston’s massive deadline investment change?
Not its playoff destination and certainly not its playoff result.
Adley Rutschman Didn’t Deliver When Boston Needed Him Most
This was the stage for which Boston acquired Rutschman.
Instead, the Red Sox scored two runs in two games.
Rutschman finished the series 1-for-8 with three strikeouts and did not drive in a run as Boston’s offense was overwhelmed by Cam Schlittler and Max Fried.
And one of his most consequential moments came defensively during Boston’s disastrous sixth inning Wednesday.
With the Red Sox trailing 2-1 and desperately trying to keep their season alive, Spencer Jones reached first after swinging at a third strike from Garrett Crochet that got away from Rutschman.
Jones then stole second and advanced to third when Rutschman’s throw sailed into center field.
George Lombard Jr. followed with an RBI single.
The inning disintegrated from there.
By the time Boston finally recorded the third out, New York had scored six runs and transformed a one-run elimination game into another rout.
It would be ridiculous to blame Rutschman for Boston’s elimination. The Red Sox were comprehensively outplayed, their offense disappeared and their pitching couldn’t contain New York when the series was on the line.
But that’s precisely why the trade deserves scrutiny.
Boston didn’t surrender a collection of valuable young players for another complementary piece.
It paid for a difference-maker.
When the difference needed to be made, it wasn’t.
Look at What Boston Gave Baltimore
The price looks even more jarring now.
Baltimore received five players:
RHP Anthony Eyanson: Boston’s No. 2 prospect at the time of the trade and a top-50 prospect in baseball. He immediately became Baltimore’s top-ranked prospect.
RHP Kyson Witherspoon: Another highly regarded pitching prospect who immediately became one of the better prospects in Baltimore’s system.
OF Enddy Azocar: A promising young outfielder who added another high-upside asset to Baltimore’s farm system.
C Carlos Narváez: Boston’s starting major-league catcher, giving Baltimore an immediate replacement behind the plate.
OF Harold Rivas: The 18-year-old outfielder eventually sent to Baltimore as the player to be named later.
Boston received Rutschman, catcher Jake Rogers and cash.
Four prospects and a starting major-league catcher.
Sent directly to an American League East rival.
That’s not a routine deadline upgrade.
That’s a significant transfer of organizational value made specifically because Boston believed Rutschman could help it win immediately.
The immediate payoff?
Thirty-two regular-season games and a postseason that lasted two losses.
The Yankees Were Offered Adley Rutschman, Too. They Walked Away.
This is where Boston’s decision becomes even harder to swallow.
The Red Sox weren’t the only AL East contender that discussed Rutschman with Baltimore.
The Yankees reportedly explored acquiring him before the deadline.
According to the New York Post, Baltimore’s asking price from New York included pitching prospect Elmer Rodríguez, catcher Austin Wells, outfield prospect Yostin Pena and either Will Warren or Ryan Weathers.
The Yankees decided it was too much.
Boston decided its own massive prospect package wasn’t.
Two months later, the teams met in October.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox.
That alone doesn’t prove New York made the correct long-term decision. Prospects fail. Rutschman could return to All-Star form. The careers of the players Boston and New York retained or surrendered will ultimately determine how these decisions age.
But the immediate comparison couldn’t be much uglier for Breslow.
New York kept its catcher.
It kept its prospects.
It kept its young pitching.
And it eliminated the team that paid Baltimore’s price.
Ben Rice Made the Comparison Even More Painful
There is another piece of this that Boston probably doesn’t want to think about.
The Yankees didn’t merely decline to acquire Rutschman.
They watched one of their own young players become the kind of offensive weapon Boston hoped it was acquiring.
Ben Rice erupted for 41 home runs during the regular season.
Then he opened the postseason by destroying the Red Sox.
Rice went 4-for-5 with two home runs and six RBIs in New York’s 9-0 Game 1 victory.
Six RBIs.
Boston scored two runs in the entire series.
The Yankees didn’t need to surrender a massive package to Baltimore to find an impact bat.
They developed one.
Boston went shopping for an established star.
Then Rice helped send its expensive new catcher and the rest of the Red Sox home.
Boston Didn’t Even Get the Superstar Version of Rutschman
Boston can at least point to Rutschman’s impressive résumé.
He was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 MLB Draft, became the centerpiece of Baltimore’s rebuild and developed into one of baseball’s most recognizable catchers.
But the Red Sox weren’t trading for his résumé.
They were trading for what he could do in 2026 and 2027.
That’s an important distinction.
Rutschman was already on the injured list with wrist inflammation when Boston acquired him.
Once healthy, he played 32 regular-season games for the Red Sox and hit .222 with a .278 on-base percentage and .410 slugging percentage.
His OPS was .688.
He hit five home runs and drove in 13 runs.
His 92 OPS+ meant he was eight percent below league average offensively after adjusting for league and ballpark conditions.
Boston surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for an immediate upgrade and received below-average regular-season offense.
Then came October.
No transformational performance.
No postseason victory.
No series win.
Craig Breslow Made a Win-Now Trade. Boston Didn’t Win.
There is nothing inherently wrong with trading prospects.
Contending organizations sometimes become too protective of players who have never taken a major-league at-bat. Windows close. Players get hurt. Rosters change.
When an organization has an opportunity to win a championship, there are times when being aggressive is exactly the right approach.
But here’s the other side of that philosophy:
If you’re going to make a win-now trade, eventually you have to win now.
Breslow pushed a significant portion of Boston’s prospect capital into the middle of the table.
The Red Sox responded by finishing 87-75.
Then they arrived at Yankee Stadium and were outscored 18-2 in two games.
That’s not an October run.
That’s barely an October appearance.
The Yankees advanced. Boston went home before October was two days old.
And the player Breslow acquired as his blockbuster deadline upgrade produced neither the offensive impact nor the postseason difference Boston was paying for.
Meanwhile, Baltimore Gets to Keep All Five Players
This is the part that could hurt Boston considerably longer than Wednesday night’s loss.
Baltimore doesn’t need all four prospects to become stars for this trade to sting the Red Sox.
It doesn’t even need two of them to become stars.
If Eyanson develops into a quality major-league starter, or Witherspoon reaches his upside, or Azocar or Rivas eventually develops into an everyday player, Boston could spend years watching a division rival benefit from its deadline gamble.
Narváez is already a major-league catcher.
The Orioles essentially converted one player approaching his final season of club control into five assets.
Boston acquired the short-term star.
Baltimore acquired years of potential value.
And the Orioles didn’t have to wait long to see the first part of their gamble work.
Rutschman’s first postseason with Boston lasted two games.
Now Boston May Have to Pay for Rutschman Again
That’s what makes this more than simply a failed 2026 deadline gamble.
Rutschman can become a free agent after the 2027 season.
Boston therefore has another major decision coming.
The Red Sox can attempt to sign him to a lucrative extension, committing significant long-term money to a catcher whose offensive production has declined from his early-career peak and who has dealt with injuries.
They can let him play out 2027 and risk watching him depart as a free agent roughly 17 months after surrendering four prospects and Narváez to acquire him.
Or they can eventually trade him and attempt to recover some of the organizational value they sent Baltimore.
None looks particularly attractive this morning.
And Boston should be especially careful about allowing the enormous acquisition cost to influence its next decision.
The prospects are gone regardless.
Paying Rutschman a huge extension because Boston already paid dearly to acquire him would be classic sunk-cost thinking.
The next decision has to be based on what Rutschman is likely to provide going forward, not what Boston surrendered to get him.
He could make this entire discussion look foolish next season. Rutschman is talented enough to rebound, produce another All-Star season and become an important part of a championship contender.
But that’s a 2027 argument.
We know what happened in 2026.
Boston was already headed toward the postseason.
Baltimore put an enormous price on Rutschman.
The Yankees looked at that price and walked away.
The Red Sox paid it.
Then those two teams met in October.
New York outscored Boston 18-2, swept the Red Sox in two games and advanced without Aaron Judge.
Boston went home.
And Baltimore still has all five players.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Roman Anthony’s Hand Injury Reveals Darker Truth For Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Spencer Rickles
item.description: The worst news for Boston fans isn't that Roman Anthony is hurt. It is that the injury is worse than anyone thought. New scans revealed fresh muscle strains in his wrist alongside old damage. This changes everything for the Red Sox playoff hopes. Scans Show Worse Damage Anthony left Game 1 of the Wild Card Series with soreness after a checked swing. He struck out twice before getting pulled in a 9-0 loss. Manager Chad Tracy said the player was sent back to Boston for more imaging. The results we
item.content:encoded:
The worst news for Boston fans isn't that Roman Anthony is hurt. It is that the injury is worse than anyone thought. New scans revealed fresh muscle strains in his wrist alongside old damage. This changes everything for the Red Sox playoff hopes.
Scans Show Worse Damage
Anthony left Game 1 of the Wild Card Series with soreness after a checked swing. He struck out twice before getting pulled in a 9-0 loss. Manager Chad Tracy said the player was sent back to Boston for more imaging. The results were grim. "We sent him back to Boston for extra, additional imaging which actually revealed some new strains to different muscles in his wrist in addition to exasperating the old injuries. It's not great," Tracy told reporters, per ESPN.
This isn't a minor tweak. The 22-year-old missed 101 games earlier this year with a torn ligament in his right ring finger. He only played 55 regular season games before this latest setback. His stats dropped from a .292 average last year to .245 this season. The Red Sox signed him to a massive $130 million extension hoping for a star. Now that deal looks like a gamble on a broken body.
A Brutal Playoff Rule
There is a cruel twist in the rulebook that fans need to know. If a player gets removed from a playoff roster during a series, he cannot play in the next series either. This means Anthony won't just miss Game 2 against the Yankees. He will be ineligible for the entire ALDS if Boston advances. The team replaced Anthony on the roster with Curtis Mead, according to MLB Trade Rumors.
Tracy tried to frame it as a common issue for players coming off long layoffs. "He's obviously coming off that. You'll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something — it's fine, it goes away," Tracy said. But the reality is different today. "Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable," he added, per ESPN. The hope is gone. The pain is real.
The Cost of a Broken Star
The Red Sox are one loss from elimination. They need every bat they can get. Jahmai Jones is set to hit leadoff as the designated hitter. The lineup includes Adley Rutschman, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu. Sonny Gray will start on the mound against a former team. But the lineup is missing its most promising young hitter.
Anthony was supposed to be the centerpiece of the next decade. His wrist issues have already cost the team almost four months of the regular season. Now they lose him in the playoffs too. The $130 million contract is secure, but the on-field value is gone for now. Boston has to hope Mead or Seigler can step up immediately. The clock is ticking, and the scans say time is not on their side.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Sonny Gray unable to keep Red Sox season alive in season-ending loss to Yankees in Game 2 of AL Wild Card Series - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tara Sullivan

The brash statement might have been out of character for the relatively soft-spoken pitcher, but the hard feelings? Those were hard earned, borne from Gray’s disastrous two-season stint in New York, a 2017-18 swing through the worst performance of an otherwise all-star caree
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Sonny Gray, upon being traded to the Red Sox, had just the right words to win over the Boston fan base.
“It feels good for me to go to a place where it’s easy to hate the Yankees,” Gray memorably said in December.
The brash statement might have been out of character for the relatively soft-spoken pitcher, but the hard feelings? Those were hard earned, borne from Gray’s disastrous two-season stint in New York, a 2017-18 swing through the worst performance of an otherwise all-star career.
Gray was like an alien dropped on a foreign planet, so uncomfortable under New York’s big-city lights, so reviled by the home fans who booed him non-stop by the end of his tenure, that it seemed he might never rediscover the dominance he had shown in small-market Oakland.
He did, resurrecting his career through stops in Cincinnati, Minnesota, and St. Louis, earning his place once again among the league’s best starters and landing him squarely on the Red Sox’ offseason radar. The front office liked him enough to request he waive a no-trade clause to join their ongoing rebuild. Gray’s memorable line after saying “yes” was a way of reminding himself of all he had done to make that union possible.
And Wednesday, here were those damn Yankees again, this time looming across the diamond at Yankee Stadium, the only thing between Gray, his Red Sox, and a long, cold winter. Words weren’t going to do it this time. Gray was going to have to pitch his way past the Yankees to keep the Red Sox’ season alive, the key to staving off elimination after the Sox were laughed out of Game 1, 9-0.
“The season’s on the line for us and he can handle that,” manager Chad Tracy said.
Gray wound up allowing two runs on six hits over 4⅔ innings, pulled after 70 pitches when Ben Rice began Gray’s third run through the Yankees order with a single. Gray surrendered a solo homer to Luis García Jr. in the fourth inning to open the scoring, but as on Tuesday, things truly came apart against the bullpen, resulting in a season-ending 9-2 setback.
The man who tookthe mound in Game 2 was so far removed from the shell of his former self who departed New York in 2019, recording one of the best seasons of his life this year for the Sox. Gray’s 18-5 record with a 2.72 ERA and 149 strikeouts in 29 starts anchored a rotation that was without injured ace Garrett Crochet for most of the regular season. Gray’s 36-year-old wisdom and experience, not to mention his maniacal work ethic, helped mold a young staff. To top it off with a playoff game in New York is like a gift from the redemption gods.
Gray was indefensibly awful during his tortured tenure in New York. He appeared in 41 games, making 34 starts before being demoted to the bullpen toward the end of his second season. His overall ERA was 4.51, an even uglier 5.26 in the 23 starts he made in 2018. The Yankees traded him to the Reds in January 2019. He has spent the time since then not simply regaining his form, but analyzing his failures.
“That’s a good question and it’s a fair question,” he said Tuesday. “It’s one of those things that you have a snowball … and there’s a snowball that kind of starts rolling down a hill. If you don’t ever stop it, then the snowball just gets bigger and bigger and bigger, and it picks up traction and it just gets more snow. And it just continues to go down this thing. And the bigger the snowball gets, the harder it is to stop it or take a step back.
“And for me, it just took me to get away and get myself into a different environment and then reflect on those things, reflect on what was good, what was bad, what didn’t work. And that took some time.
“But I do know that playing here made me a stronger person, made me a better man, a better husband. Ultimately, it made me a better pitcher, a better baseball player. And that’s kind of what I take from my time here.”
Ultimately, Gray expressed gratitude for his time in New York.
“I think there’s a lot of people and a lot of players that can have one bump in the road and not get back on the tracks,” he said, “and for me, there’s been bumps along the way and that may have been a little bit of a bigger bump than others. But then to be able to recenter, to refocus, to continue to have confidence in yourself and not get off the wagon, get back on the wagon and continue to move forward in your career and in your life as well … ultimately it made me a better person.”
Gray relied on all of those skills as he navigated this utterly unpredictable, wholly unexpected Red Sox season. From the early-season firing of manager Alex Cora to the midseason catching change to Adley Rutschman, from the April and May cellar-dwelling standings to the remarkable 15-game winning streak and playoff turnaround, Gray told me earlier this season, “It’s been quite the journey. I’ve never been part of anything like this.”
Tara Sullivan is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at tara.sullivan@globe.com. Follow her @Globe_Tara.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Cody Bellinger takes Chad Tracy's gift, ends Red Sox season in Yankees legacy moment
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib

On Wednesday night, with a chance to end the Red Sox season in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, and with his champion dad Clay in the building (first pitch duties), he responded directly to Sox manager Chad Tracy opening the door with a pair of punishing blows. Payton To
item.content:encoded:
Though Cody Bellinger didn't spend much of his childhood in the new Yankee Stadium, that should've been all the more motivation for him to join the Yankees and make this place sound like the old one as often as he possibly could. On Wednesday night, with a chance to end the Red Sox season in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, and with his champion dad Clay in the building (first pitch duties), he responded directly to Sox manager Chad Tracy opening the door with a pair of punishing blows.
Payton Tolle getting the 83-pitch early hook in Game 1 was somewhat defensible. He was losing grip. He's past a career high in innings. They have the horses. Removing Sonny Gray from this do-or-die game before the end of the fifth inning, midway through a masterpiece, was one of the silliest bits of overmanaging you'll see. Bringing in Erik Miller, who was victimized with two outs in the fifth in Game 1 to get victimized again was even sillier.
Bellinger smoked a two-out RBI single off Miller to add a second run to the Yankees' lead. The next time he strode to the plate, he made a much larger impact.
Cody Bellinger cements Yankees' ownership of the Boston Red Sox
Gone. Very gone. In a snap, the Yankees turned two productive outs and a three-run mash into an 8-1 ballgame. Losing Garrett Whitlock, who surrendered the bomb, might've been the Yankees' most prudent Rule 5 Draft move in franchise history. It's called the long game.
For those keeping track at home, the 2026 Red Sox rode a 32-5 midsummer stretch to the postseason, reached within a half-game of the Yankees and got high on their own supply. From that point forward, they were much closer to .500, losing impact role players and stars alike by the bowlful. Sox fans were undeterred. They continued to crow. They loved to laugh at Aaron Judge's injury troubles. They purported to be inside Cam Schlittler's head. If they truly were in there, they might've been able to pick up some knowledge on what it takes for a pitcher to go deep into games in the postseason and dominate.
And so, for the second season in a row, the Yankees have flushed the Sox out of the postseason - Boston actually doesn't even reach October this year, which begins tomorrow. Last year, it was Schlittler, the Massachusetts native, growing up on the big stage. He helped this year, too.
But this time around, it ended with Tracy hooking Gray for no apparent reason and Bellinger, a son of pinstripes, delivering the crushing blow. Maybe, just maybe, order has returned to the universe and karma has begun to punish the brashness of Bostonians in new and unique ways. Whitlock gagging, Garrett Crochet disintegrating after an Adley Rutschman slow play (the trade target the Sox outbid the Yankees for, by the way), and Caleb Durbin making the final out ... in a game Gray should've owned ... was a pretty clever way to get it done.
Thanks, Belli.

item.title: [wral.com] Fried, Bellinger and García lead Yankees over Red Sox 9-2 for 2-game Wild Card Series sweep
item.dc:creator: RONALD BLUM
item.description: NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston. Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep. Other WRAL Top Stories “We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said. New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series start
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston.
Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep.
Other WRAL Top Stories
“We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.
“The fans were electric from the first pitch and the boys were hungry. We got a young, hungry team here," Yankees captain Aaron Judge said as teammates sprayed him with bubbly during the clubhouse celebration. “This makes me feel young every single time.”
Judge missed this series because of a calf injury and isn't sure whether he will play against the Rays, who beat New York 7-6 in the season series.
“Saturday’s a long ways away," he said.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston's 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke open the game with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out leading off — with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBIs that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst that put New York ahead 8-1.
“Step one,” said Bellinger, who caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay, a 2000 Yankees World Series champion. “Now we got to go into Tampa and play against a tough team."
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, lost last year's wild-card matchup after defeating the Yankees in the opener.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there was quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series and that ended for us tonight, so it’s frustrating,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “There’s a lot of things you can say, but in the moment right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it’s going to take some time to get over that.”
Boston, which also got a seventh-inning homer from Nick Sogard off Will Warren, was missing leadoff hitter Roman Anthony because of a hand injury. The Red Sox were held to a .117 average in the series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and outscored 18-2.
New York hit .382 in the series. Boston's bullpen had a 20.25 ERA.
“We played great baseball in a lot of ways here, obviously anchored by our two great starters," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
Yankees batters hit .450 (9 for 20) with runners in scoring position after finishing 19th among the 30 teams with a .246 RISP during the regular season.
“I feel like it’s a whole new level from regular season to these last two days,” Austin Wells said.
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García's fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just relieved.
Gray was disappointed he wasn't allowed to face Bellinger.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that’s a fact,” Gray said. "I would’ve liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. And, yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. So I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted.”
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, throwing error, stolen base, bunt single and intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger's homer.
"I can’t believe they were willing to face a guy like Belli with men on base there," Rice said.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year's Wild Card Series opener, hadn't pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation when he bounced a sweeper off Adley Rutschman's chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled that Jones was out. The Yankees appealed and the call was reversed by the video umpire at the commissioner's office.
“I couldn’t believe he was there,” Boone said. "I saw the ball squirt away a little bit. I didn’t think that much of it, and looked up and I was, like, 'Oh, he’s safe.'''
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Wells' sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout and Rice, who had four hits and six RBIs in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats.
Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“Definitely wasn’t sharp from the get-go but just wanted to challenge them, not try to give any free passes, especially in the first inning," Fried said.
After a night of celebration and a day off, the Yankees will head to Florida on Friday.
“There’s just so much more to do,” Bellinger said after the big night with his father on hand. “So obviously enjoy the moment, understand how cool it is, but keep on going.”
Up Next
New York RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.
___
See AP’s full MLB coverage here

item.title: [bostonherald.com] Cerullo: Garrett Crochet’s big return turns into a Red Sox nightmare
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: NEW YORK — When the Red Sox activated Garrett Crochet and included him on their postseason roster, they no doubt hoped that when he eventually took the mound it would be to protect a late lead and help lock down a crucial playoff win. item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — When the Red Sox activated Garrett Crochet and included him on their postseason roster, they no doubt hoped that when he eventually took the mound it would be to protect a late lead and help lock down a crucial playoff win.
They didn’t have anything like the nightmare that unfolded Wednesday in mind.
Crochet finally took the mound for the first time since April 25 with the Red Sox trailing 2-1 in the sixth inning. Boston had just scored on a Willson Contreras solo homer, breaking up the club’s marathon streak of 26.2 consecutive scoreless postseason innings dating back to Game 2 of last fall’s Wild Card Series.
Even a one-run deficit felt daunting with the way the Red Sox have been hitting since the start of September, so it was incumbent on Crochet to keep the Yankees from getting any further ahead.
Things started off well enough — Crochet’s first pitch was a 97 mph sinker to Spencer Jones — but then the storybook moment fell apart.
Crochet struck Jones out with a filthy sweeper, but Adley Rutschman couldn’t handle it and Jones reached on the dropped third strike. He then stole second, took third on Rutschman’s throwing error and scored on George Lombard Jr.’s ensuing RBI single. Things snowballed from there with three straight hits, and before Crochet knew what hit him the bases were loaded with nobody out, and manager Chad Tracy was coming out to summon Garrett Whitlock to put out the fire.
Everyone came around to score, and when Cody Bellinger took Whitlock deep for a three-run home run to make it 8-1, the Red Sox were well and truly cooked en route to a season-ending 9-2 loss.
Crochet’s final line: four batters faced, four runs scored, no outs recorded.
“It sucks. Personally to think that I busted my (butt) for the past five months for it to end that way, on a personal note it’s tough,” Crochet said postgame. “I just wanted to come back and contribute to the team as best as I could and I let them down.”
In the end, Boston’s late arriving reinforcements proved too little, too late.
Even if Crochet had pitched a perfect sixth inning, it was abundantly clear throughout the series that the Yankees were the better team. Only one team’s starting pitchers worked deep into the ballgame, and only one team’s lineup consistently came through with timely hits and back-breaking home runs.
That sure wasn’t the Red Sox, so if there’s one silver lining Crochet can take away, it’s that he at least got his opportunity to turn the tide after grinding through five months of recovery and rehab from his nagging shoulder injury.
Though in the immediate aftermath, Crochet certainly didn’t feel that way.
“It was definitely nice to touch again, it’s hard to find a lot of positives to take when you don’t record an out,” Crochet said. “I felt like I was in control as much as you can be when you’re getting the (expletive) beat out of you, but at the end of the day I did what I wanted to do out there and it wasn’t good enough. That’s really all it is.”
That’s more than Curtis Mead can say.
Acquired prior to the trade deadline from the Washington Nationals in exchange for Connelly Early, Mead was brought to Boston specifically to fortify the Red Sox lineup for big games like this one. Mead suffered a fractured left wrist in his first game with the club after being hit by a pitch, but over the past week he finally turned the corner in his recovery and was activated as an injury replacement for Roman Anthony ahead of Game 2.
Prior to the game Mead spoke about how special it was getting to suit up for a playoff game, admitting that not long ago he didn’t think he’d be back in time.
“Probably two weeks ago if you asked if I thought I’d be in this position, the answer would probably be no,” Mead said. “So it’s definitely exciting.”
Mead did not appear in Wednesday’s loss, but had the Red Sox forced a decisive Game 3 there is a chance Mead might have had a chance to start, most likely as the designated hitter in Anthony’s place. Would he have fared any better than Crochet in his return? He only just faced live pitching for the first time during Monday’s team workout at Yankee Stadium, when he squared off against rookie left-hander Tyler Samaniego in a live batting practice session.
Before that, he’d just hit off the Trajekt machine — a state-of-the-art pitching machine that mimics actual big leaguers — for the first time on Saturday at Tropicana Field.
In many respects, that super accelerated ramp-up mirrored Crochet’s return to action.
Like Mead, the Red Sox ace couldn’t get back on the field until after the minor league season was over. That meant a rehab assignment wasn’t on the table, so if either of them were going to come back there was inevitably going to be some element of being tossed back into the fire.
Even for a pitcher of Crochet’s caliber, jumping right into the boiling cauldron that is Yankee Stadium a few outs from a playoff series victory was always going to be a Hail Mary.
While the Baseball Gods have answered Boston’s prayers in the postseason before, this year it just wasn’t meant to be.
“These guys grinded all year long, I think that we’re maybe a little undeserving of the fate we got but sometimes that’s the game,” Crochet said. “Sometimes it’s good, sometimes it’s (expletive), sometimes you do all the right things and it doesn’t go your way. Ultimately they executed at a higher clip than us and that’s the game.”

item.title: [NBC Sports Boston] What we learned: Chad Tracy, bullpen and historically bad offense sink Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Michael Hurley
item.description: Heading into the Wild Card Series, one could make a case that the Red Sox had a chance to beat the Yankees.
