item.content:encoded:
Heading into the Wild Card Series, one could make a case that the Red Sox had a chance to beat the Yankees. It would take two or three great starts from Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and/or Ranger Suarez, it would take some timely hitting to put two or three runs on the board per game, and it would take some lockdown relief innings from the back end of the bullpen.
Yet the Red Sox only got decent starts from Tolle and Gray, they set a new franchise record for offensive utility, and their bullpen was a catastrophe.
And the cherry on top was that their manager, who inked a contract extension last week, showed he certainly does not know how to manage in the postseason.
Other than that, did you enjoy the series?
Here's everything we learned from the ever-so-brief two-game sweep in the Wild Card Series, as the 2026 team technically failed to get as far as the 2025 Red Sox.
Red Sox set ugly new franchise record
Red Sox history spans 126 seasons, so it was a bit surprising to see the broadcast note early in Game 2 that Boston was in the midst of rewriting franchise history with the longest scoring drought to start a postseason ever.
Obviously, the Red Sox' offense has been stagnant (or worse) for weeks, but 26 previous trips to the playoffs, you'd figure that they had started off with a scoreless game and a half before.
Alas, nope. This drought was historic. It ended at 14.2 innings, broken by Willson Contreras' solo shot with two outs in the sixth inning.
And while some of it may be explained by the absences of Roman Anthony and Mickey Gasper, there's no excuse for a playoff team to be this helpless at the plate.
Chad Tracy is not a big-game manager right now
There may have been a case for Chad Tracy to pull Payton Tolle for Erik Miller in Game 1. Not really, but there could have been a case made for Miller's sinker being more effective against Ben Rice than Tolle's fastball.
Yet there's simply no way to understand why one night later, Tracy made the exact same move.
With Sonny Gray at just 70 pitches and the Yankees leading 1-0 with two outs in the fifth inning, Tracy went back to Miller, this time with two runners on base and Cody Bellinger at the plate. The left-left matchup was presumably the reason for the call, but Bellinger crushes sliders from lefties. And when Miller threw a slider to Bellinger ... he delivered.
Bellinger singled home a run, and Miller then gave up another hit to Luis Garcia Jr. The Red Sox only got out of the inning because Rice was caught at home after an aggressive send on that second single.
Gray's pitch count of 70 was tied for his second-lowest of the season, and though he had allowed two singles in the fifth, his body of work over the season and over the past 13 years gave him a much better chance of escaping the mini jam than Miller, who had a 2.045 WHIP and 7.36 ERA in the month of September and who gave up a home run and a single while getting just one out the night before.
If Tracy was insistent that Gray had to come out of the game, he had, quite literally, every high-leverage arm available to him. Instead, he went with Erik Miller.
And with that same complement of arms available in the bottom of the sixth inning, Tracy went with Garrett Crochet, who hasn't pitched in a game since April 25. It didn't go well.
Tracy also showed a lack of feel for the moment when he let leadoff hitter Jahmai Jones, who batted .129 with a .432 OPS over the final 13 games of the regular season and who struck out looking twice, to take his third at-bat in the sixth inning, with the Red Sox trailing 2-0.
Given Boston's offensive ineptitude, the bullpen decisions are perhaps all moot. But had this been a close series, or if the Red Sox find themselves in one in the future, Tracy will carry some major doubt regarding his ability to manage those games.
Simply put, Chad Tracy did not do a single thing right in these two high-stakes games.
More Red Sox Coverage
Luis Garcia Jr.'s home run was great hitting, not bad pitching
It took until the fourth inning for the Yankees to get to Sonny Gray, but the solo homer he allowed to Luis Garcia Jr. didn't come on a bad pitch at all.
Leading off the fourth, Garcia was behind in the count 1-2 when Gray tried to bury a sweeper down and in to the lefty. Gray hit his spot with a pitch that was set to hit the bottom of the strike zone. But Garcia simply stayed on the pitch and went down and got it.
Luis Gar-SEE-YA 🦁 pic.twitter.com/GqxScAqskG
— New York Yankees (@Yankees) October 1, 2026
With the Red Sox starved for runs, Garcia's solo shot was a jarring reminder that all it takes is one good swing to put a run on the board.
Boston eventually got that swing from Contreras in the sixth, but that jolt of hope for the visiting team didn't last long.
What could have been with Garrett Crochet ...
If you just looked at the box score, you'd be shocked to see Garrett Crochet's line. He faced four batters, allowing all of them to score. He didn't record an out, despite getting Spencer Jones to chase strike three to start the sixth inning.
Of course, some of that outcome was fair, as Crochet allowed back-to-back singles. But Caleb Durbin couldn't get the out at first on what was intended to be a sacrifice bunt, Crochet left with the bases loaded, and Garrett Whitlock -- who had a dreadful night -- couldn't limit the damage at all.
Such an outcome was perhaps expected, considering Crochet has not pitched in a game since April 25 due to shoulder problems. But you also can't help but wonder what would have happened if Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras hadn't combined to bungle Crochet's inning-opening strikeout of Jones.
Rutschman took an extra beat to pounce on the ball that had bounced off his chest, and then he took an extra step before firing to first base. There, Contreras was planted on the back side of the base instead of the front. As a result, Jones was able to beat the throw.
Credit to Aaron Boone for challenging that call, which was initially an out on the field, but really, it wasn't even close.
Rutschman then compounded the matter by sailing a throw into center field when Jones stole second, allowing the runner to take third before scoring on a single. Had Rutschman made either of those two throws, it's fair to wonder how differently Crochet's inning could have gone.
Summing up the season
There will be plenty of time in the coming months to eulogize this season, but really, despite the 32-5 stretch in the summer, it wasn't one to celebrate.
Last year's team won a game in the Wild Card Series, a disappointing ending. This year's team couldn't even do that.
Injuries to Crochet and Anthony were certainly impactful, but this roster -- and particularly the offense -- was not built to contend for a World Series. The Red Sox scored two or fewer runs in 13 of their final 23 games, averaging 2.5 runs per game over that stretch.
With the season on the line, the Red Sox had Jahmai Jones, Nate Eaton and Nick Sogard in their starting lineup.
After trading three of their top-five prospects to acquire Adley Rutschman, the catcher batted .222 with a .688 OPS in the regular season before going 1-for-8 in the playoffs.
Willson Contreras, a 34-year-old former catcher with a lot of MLB miles on him, was worn down by the end of the season. Caleb Durbin, whose lows outnumbered his highs this year, went 0-for-7 in the playoffs. Ceddanne Rafaela posted the same numbers, too.
The return for Marcelo Mayer was Erik Miller, who made a strong first impression but played a pivotal role in sinking the team's chances in both postseason losses after an extremely unreliable final month of the season.
The starting pitching staff was excellent, and the bullpen was elite. But the overall roster construction will lead to plenty of questions about Craig Breslow's ability to build a real winner. Likewise, the two playoff games cast some serious doubt on whether Chad Tracy is a manager capable of winning games in October.
The 15-game winning streak and 32-5 stretch might have led to some internal victory laps and the decisions to stick with Breslow and Tracy for the foreseeable future. But the 2026 Red Sox, on the whole, were what they were: mediocre. And having been stuck in mediocrity (or worse) for half a decade, there won't be much more patience in and around Boston for it to continue.
Technically, the historic season turnaround may have been a positive, as making the playoffs beats bottoming out more often than not. But considering that the Red Sox likely could have loaded up on promising players by selling off veteran pieces like Contreras, Gray, Aroldis Chapman and anyone else at the deadline, that run in July may have hurt the Red Sox in the long term -- especially with the prospect haul that went out to acquire Rutschman.
In any event, the Red Sox finished as the third-best team in the AL East, and they failed to win a single playoff game, getting outscored 18-2 in their lone playoff series. That's the final word on the season as the long offseason -- potentially longer than most -- awaits.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Sonny Gray's premature exit curses Chad Tracy, Red Sox into brutal Wild Card ending

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox fans didn't want to see Chad Tracy emerge from the dugout in the bottom of the fifth inning. He should've learned from his Game 1 mistake.
But in Wild Card Game 2, Tracy pulled Sonny Gray after 4.2 frames to swap him for Erik Miller, just as he did with Payton Tolle the day before. Gray was having a better night than Tolle, though — he collected five strikeouts and allowed two runs on six hits. He was living on the edges and racked up swing-and-miss through 70 pitches.
Miller entered the game and immediately let up a single to Cody Bellinger. The Yankees took a 2-0 lead. The run was charged to Gray, but it didn't have to be that way. Miller posted a brutal September and struggled similarly in his first Wild Card outing. The choice to turn to him again, especially with the season on the line, is inexplicable.
Tracy's bullpen management didn't get any better. Garrett Crochet entered the game in the sixth inning and immediately got unlucky. Spencer Jones struck out swinging at a pitch in the dirt and Adley Rutschman couldn't get a good block on it, which allowed Jones to take first base. Crochet pitched decently well, avoiding the middle of the plate, but he couldn't collect an out before New York plated another run and loaded the bases.
Chad Tracy pulling Sonny Gray early led to the Red Sox's downfall in Wild Card Game 2, as it did in Game 1 with Payton Tolle
Going to Crochet while the game was still within reach was another strange choice by Tracy. Crochet hadn't pitched in the big leagues since April 25 due to two different shoulder injuries — the Red Sox had no idea how he would fare in a game, but went to him anyway despite having Jake Bennett available.
Tracy's bullpen management choices certainly didn't make the Red Sox any better this series, but their offense deserves some blame for the way the Wild Card series went. Willson Contreras and Nick Sogard contributed solo home runs to prevent another shutout, but no one else gave them any help. Four hits, seven strikeouts and 0-for-2 with runners in scoring position won't cut it against any playoff team, let alone the Yankees' utterly dominant pitching staff.
Even so, Boston got more offense in the win-or-go-home game than it did in Game 1, and bad bullpen management did the Red Sox in again. Had Tracy kept Gray in the game, the score could've stayed closer and the game might've actually been winnable. Instead, an incredible, memorable season came to an end without ever reaching October, and the Red Sox did it to themselves.

item.title: [wcvb.com] Roman Anthony out of Red Sox lineup in Game 2 of Wild Card Series against Yankees after hurting hand
item.dc:creator: Imani Clement
item.description: Red Sox's Roman Anthony diagnosed with right hand strain, ineligible to return until ALCS The Red Sox announced that Roman Anthony would not be in the Boston Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of their AL Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees on Wednesday night, a day after leaving the opener because of hand pain. In a statement on Wednesday, the team announced that Anthony was diagnosed with a right-hand strain and was substituted off the roster. Anthony can no longer participate in the remainde
item.content:encoded:
Red Sox's Roman Anthony diagnosed with right hand strain, ineligible to return until ALCS
The Red Sox announced that Roman Anthony would not be in the Boston Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of their AL Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees on Wednesday night, a day after leaving the opener because of hand pain.
In a statement on Wednesday, the team announced that Anthony was diagnosed with a right-hand strain and was substituted off the roster.
Anthony can no longer participate in the remainder of the Wild Card Series or the American League Division Series if Boston advances.
He would be eligible to return for the American League Championship Series.
"I feel sick to my stomach. I haven't slept much. It doesn't feel real, to be honest," Anthony said Wednesday. "I been through so many emotions and feelings to get the same news again and even worse, it's hard to have an answer to anything right now."
The team announced that infielder Curtis Mead will replace Anthony on the Wild Card Series roster.
Anthony said he wasn't sure what the treatment plan would be currently to remedy his hand injury.
"Once we decided I wasn't going to play today, that's all that really mattered," Anthony said. "All that mattered was putting the team in the best situation to win."
Batting leadoff as a designated hitter in his playoff debut Tuesday, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against Cam Schlittler before getting lifted for a pinch hitter with his team trailing by two runs in the sixth inning of a 9-0 loss.
Boston manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings. The 22-year-old Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29 with an injury to the same hand.
"Unfortunately, I checked swing on my second at-bat and I knew right then and there it was time to get it looked and put somebody else in the game that would have a better chance to win," Anthony said.
“He’s obviously coming off that. You’ll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something — it’s fine, it goes away,” Tracy said. “Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable.”
Jahmai Jones was set to hit leadoff as the DH with the Red Sox one loss from elimination, followed in the batting order by catcher Adley Rutschman, first baseman Willson Contreras, right fielder Wilyer Abreu, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, third baseman Caleb Durbin, second baseman Nick Sogard, shortstop Trevor Story and left fielder Nate Eaton.
Sonny Gray was set to start on the mound for Boston against one of his former teams.
One of baseball’s premier prospects when he debuted last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBIs and a .735 OPS in 55 games this season.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.content:encoded:
Lost amid the embarrassing madness of Tuesday's Wild Card series opener between the Boston Red Sox and the New York Yankees was Roman Anthony being pinch-hit for midway through the game, seemingly out of nowhere. After the game, it was revealed by manager Chad Tracy that Anthony had re-aggravated the wrist injury that had kept him out for more than three months during the regular season — and that his Game 2 status was up in the air.
Well, Boston's Game 2 lineup is out, and it's safe to say the fan base won't like it, with Anthony on the bench.
Is Roman Anthony playing tonight? Red Sox's lineup gives answer
Here's a look at Boston's Anthony-less lineup against Yankees left-hander Max Fried.
| Player | Position |
|---|---|
| 1. Jahmai Jones | DH |
| 2. Adley Rutschman | C |
| 3. Willson Contreras | 1B |
| 4. Wilyer Abreu | RF |
| 5. Ceddanne Rafaela | CF |
| 6. Caleb Durbin | 3B |
| 7. Nick Sogard | 2B |
| 8. Trevor Story | SS |
| 9. Nate Eaton | LF |
Yeah, the Red Sox are going to miss Anthony dearly. Sure, there's the makings of a decent lineup here. Jahmai Jones has done nothing but crush lefties since the Red Sox acquired him. Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras are proven stars. Wilyer Abreu has broken out against left-handers this season, in particular. Ceddanne Rafaela is having his best offensive year. Still, there's no replacing Anthony.
He only appeared in 55 regular-season games and didn't look great in his two at-bats on Tuesday, but nobody in Boston's organization has a higher ceiling than Anthony. Being without him makes the already daunting challenge of rebounding from an 0-1 deficit in the best-of-three series that much more difficult.
Red Sox's growing injury report makes it tougher to believe in dream run
What makes Anthony's injury that much more difficult is that he's far from the only one. The Red Sox have a slew of notables on the IL, and that's making achieving their ultimate gol tough to believe in.
| Player | Position | Injury | Return |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mickey Gasper | C/INF | Right biceps strain | 2027 |
| Tyron Guerrero | RHP | Right shoulder strain | 2027 |
| Eli White | INF/OF | Ligament damage in right foot | 2027 |
| Curtis Mead | INF | Left wrist fracture | Postseason or 2027 |
| Kutter Crawford | RHP | Right flexor irritation | 2027 |
| Johan Oviedo | RHP | Right flexor strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Anthony Siegler | INF | Right wrist discomfort | Postseason or 2027 |
| Justin Slaten | RHP | Right elbow inflammation | 2027 |
| Masataka Yoshida | DH | Left hamstring strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Triston Casas | 1B | Left abdominal strain | 2027 |
The list is lengthy and littered with quality talent. Lineup-wise, the Red Sox sure could use Mickey Gasper, who was one of their hottest hitters before suffering his injury, right about now. They could also use Curtis Mead, a player who crushes left-handed pitching. Even Masataka Yoshida's bat would really come in handy with Anthony out.
Pitching-wise, Boston's depth has taken a hit. Tyron Guerrero and Justin Slaten are two of the most important members of their bullpen, and perhaps they would've been able to keep the game closer on Tuesday had they been healthy. Guys like Kutter Crawford and Johan Oviedo are proven back-end starters who could've eaten innings this October.
Perhaps the Red Sox can get Mead and a few others back if they can get past the Yankees, but with Anthony now joining the laundry list of injured players, it's getting tough to believe in them making a comeback.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Adley Rutschman justifies Red Sox trade with pre-playoff hot streak amid injuries and uncertainty
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: The Boston Red Sox have not entered the postseason on a high note. Not only are Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela not at 100 percent health-wise, Mickey Gasper, Eli White, Tyron Guerrero and other players are down with injuries. The Sox's offense has seriously struggled in the lead up to the postseason, as well. Boston posted a league-worst .651 OPS and 71 runs scored in September — that's 18 fewer runs than the Philadelphia Phillies, the second-worst run scoring team in the season's final
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have not entered the postseason on a high note. Not only are Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela not at 100 percent health-wise, Mickey Gasper, Eli White, Tyron Guerrero and other players are down with injuries.
The Sox's offense has seriously struggled in the lead up to the postseason, as well. Boston posted a league-worst .651 OPS and 71 runs scored in September — that's 18 fewer runs than the Philadelphia Phillies, the second-worst run scoring team in the season's final month.
But as the rest of his team has faltered, Adley Rutschman is heating up just at the right time. The former Baltimore Orioles catcher is slashing .266/.299/.547 in September, which might not seem like a huge breakout, but he batted just .170/.254/.245 in August, his first month in Boston.
Rutschman's last week is the most encouraging sign yet for the Sox. He's slashing .346/.370/.577 with a home run in his last seven games. Baseball is a game of momentum and Rutschman is one of the few Red Sox entering the Wild Card series hot. Boston will need his best work at the plate this series, especially from the right side, given the injuries it's dealing with. Thankfully, Rutschman is finally thriving from the right-handed batter's box.
Adley Rutschman is heating up for the Red Sox right at the perfect time
The Red Sox paid a hefty price for Rutschman at the trade deadline to bring a much-needed upgrade to their catcher spot. The 28-year-old is one of the best defensive catchers in the league and he effectively eliminates any advantage opposing teams have at the plate and on the base paths, a boost Connor Wong certainly doesn't bring on his start days. Now, Rutschman is finally starting to give the Sox the offensive production they hoped for when they sold all their best minor league pitchers and more for him.
Boston has rewarded Rutschman with the No. 2 spot in their Wild Card Game 1 lineup (subscription required). Manager Chad Tracy foreshadowed his placement in the lineup during the last game of the season against the Cubs, in which Rutschman went 1-for-2 with a homer and a walk. Batting him second is quite a risk, given the catcher's offensive trouble this season, but the Sox need all the help they can get at the plate and Rutschman is their hottest bat.
Rutschman doesn't have a ton of playoff experience from his tenure with the Orioles, but the five games he's played in October are more than many Sox players have under their belt. As one of their only players who's felt the pressure of the postseason on more than one occasion, the Red Sox need Rutschman to stay hot.

item.title: [si.com] The Potentially Fatal Flaw For Each MLB Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early. With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team. Brewers: Lack of Power The Brewers were baseball’s best team
item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

item.title: [Over the Monster] Chad Tracy could swing the series between the Red Sox and Yankees
item.dc:creator: Keagan Stiefel
item.description: Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series. The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of
item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman, and Caleb Durbin will join the lineup in hopes to scrape together more than the six total runs they scored last season. Crochet could end up joining the bullpen in his return from injury, along with newcomers Erik Miller and Jake Bennett, which is a pretty decent group of pitchers being added to one of the very best units in baseball this season.
The Yankees will also be in a better position on the pitching side, with Gerrit Cole serving as the do-or-die option behind Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Luis Garcia Jr., Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. should help the lineup against left-handers, though there is something to be said about the so-so status of Aaron Judge.
If we can boil all of that down, though, only one man can completely swing the series…
Chad Tracy.
Tracy’s most difficult decisions might come before the season even starts, as he will be relied upon heavily to figure out who will fill out the roster — Braiden Ward? Jarren Duran? Curtis Mead? Jahmai Jones? Nate Eaton? Isiah Kiner-Falefa? Crochet?
It’s not going to be easy, but all of that pales in comparison to making decisions with who will play, when they will play, and how he manages things when the lights are at their brightest in The Bronx.
“It’s the playoffs, so we’re at the point in the season where teams that are remaining need to win or they’re going home,” Tracy said during his media availability on Monday. “I have a feel for that.
“… It’s all hands on deck. I think everyone is aware that during the playoffs it’s about winning moments and being aggressive — all those things. I think most of our guys who have been around understand that, so we’re going to go out and play our butts off and manage and do everything we can to win each game.”
Alex Cora, the manager of last year’s squad that became the first in history to lose the best-of-three series after taking a lead, made some… interesting decisions in hindsight.
Bello was pulled after 2 1/3 innings in Game 2, which led to Justin Wilson, Zack Kelly, Garrett Whitlock, and Tolle being used out of the bullpen and becoming unavailable for Game 3. Nate Eaton started over Wilyer Abreu in Game 2. Rob Refsnyder got two starts over Masataka Yoshida, which makes sense considering they faced two left-handers, but he finished 0-for-5 while the latter went 4-for-7. Nathaniel Lowe played in all three games, while Nick Sogard only played in two.
It’s easy to go back in time and poke holes though these decisions with the benefit of hindsight, but that’s kind of the whole point in looking ahead at the same two teams playing each other again with one of them being led by someone new.
Tracy needs to avoid making similar mistakes, and he needs to do it without the benefit of years of experience in similar situations. The Red Sox stripped him of that interim tag because they believe he can, and it’s only a matter of time before we find out whether or not they’re right.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Alex Bregman went 4 for 4 with two home runs and four RBIs in his second game back from a frightening injury, and the Chicago Cubs beat the Boston Red Sox 6-2 on Sunday in a regular-season finale that was relocated to Tropicana Field.
Chicago is the No. 5 seed in the National League playoffs and will play a best-of-three Wild Card Series at fourth-seeded San Diego beginning Tuesday night.
Boston is the No. 5 seed in the American League playoffs and will travel to New York to open its Wild Card Series the same night against the rival Yankees.
Major League Baseball moved the Cubs-Red Sox season finale to Florida because of a weekend nor’easter that was expected to batter the Boston area into Monday. Ahead of the storm, the Red Sox swept a doubleheader from the Cubs on Friday at Fenway Park.
Bregman went 0 for 4 with a strikeout at designated hitter in the opener — five days after sustaining facial fractures when he was struck in the face by a foul ball while standing in the on-deck circle.
The three-time All-Star third baseman, who played for Boston last year, was the DH again Sunday and fared much better at the plate in his final postseason tuneup. In addition to finishing a triple shy of the cycle, he drew a walk and scored three times.
With the NL MVP award virtually locked up, Pete Crow-Armstrong singled to open the game before Cubs manager Craig Counsell immediately removed him for pinch-runner Tyrone Taylor. Bregman launched the next pitch from Tanner Houck (0-1) into the left-field seats.
Adley Rutschman hit a solo homer off Chicago starter Shota Imanaga, who was lifted after one inning with postseason seeding already decided.
Braxton Garrett (1-1) pitched five strong innings in relief for his first win since May 29, 2024. Colin Rea earned his second save.
Played at the home of the Tampa Bay Rays, the game drew 20,411 fans who had less than 48 hours’ notice to purchase tickets.
Chicago finished 89-73, three games shy of its 92-70 mark in 2025.
Boston, which was 89-73 in 2025, ended the season 87-75. The Red Sox fired manager Alex Cora following a 10-17 start and replaced him with Chad Tracy.
Under Tracy, Boston became the first team to qualify for the postseason after dropping as many as 44 of its initial 75 games.
___

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox Manager Chad Tracy Reveals Willson Contreras Playoff Availability
item.dc:creator: Dan Morrison
item.description: Throughout the season, first baseman Willson Contreras has been the emotional heart for the Boston Red Sox. However, he largely hasn’t been able to play in the month of September due to injuries. He spent time on the IL due to a hamstring injury. That had been bugging him for some time, and the Red Sox wanted him to reset and get healthy for the postseason. He did, but almost as soon as he came back, he was hit in the right hand by a pitch. item.content:encoded:
Throughout the season, first baseman Willson Contreras has been the emotional heart for the Boston Red Sox. However, he largely hasn’t been able to play in the month of September due to injuries.
He spent time on the IL due to a hamstring injury. That had been bugging him for some time, and the Red Sox wanted him to reset and get healthy for the postseason. He did, but almost as soon as he came back, he was hit in the right hand by a pitch. That forced Contreras to miss about a week and a half before DHing in the final game of the season on Sunday.
Boston Red Sox Manager Chad Tracy on Willson Contreras in the Playoffs
In the end, Willson Contreras had just two at-bats on Sunday. He’d go 0-2 with a strikeout before Jahmai Jones came in to pinch-hit for him.
It was a small sample size, but it was another emotional boost that Contreras could provide the Red Sox. The postseason is here and he’s healthy enough to play. Better than that, after the game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy confirmed that he should be available for the Wild Card Round in the postseason.
“He was okay,” Tracy said. “Took the first one [at-bat]. Took the second one. Had a pretty good at-bat. Hit the ball hard to third and he was good. So, I got him out of there… Should be [good to go].
Getting hit on the hand is risky, with plenty of smaller bones to break. Luckily, X-Rays showed that Contreras avoided that, and was just dealing with bad swelling that made it hard to swing a bat. He had previously been anxious about his availability for the postseason when describing it as a bone bruise.
“Yeah, there’s no fracture or anything,” Contreras said. “I had a CT scan yesterday just to make sure that I don’t have any fracture, and it didn’t show any fracture. At this point, still inflammation and a bone bruise.”
This comes at a time when the Red Sox have been desperately trying to get healthy. Players like Adley Rutschman and Caleb Durbin are banged up but playing through it. Others, like Ceddanne Rafaela and Curtis Mead, have needed to spend time on the IL.
Now, the Red Sox will turn their attention ahead to the New York Yankees. The American League Wild Card Series will begin on Tuesday, September 29th in the Bronx. First pitch is scheduled for 8:00 p.m. EST.
It’s Been a Career Season for Contreras
The frustrating part of the injuries for Contreras, other than that it could cost him time in the postseason, is that this has been a career season for him. This comes in his first year with the Red Sox as he’s brought a swing made for Fenway Park to Boston.
He’s hitting .276 with a .905 OPS. Contreras also has 27 home runs and 81 RBIs. That’s in a 129 game effort, and amounted to 4.5 WAR, per Baseball Reference.
Statistically, it’s Contreras’ best season. His previous high for WAR was 4.2 back in 2021. Otherwise, he hadn’t cracked that 4.0 WAR mark before. That was also a new single-season high for home runs and RBIs in his career. So, maybe it shouldn’t be a surprise that’s a career-record for OPS in a season, too.
The Red Sox need that version of Contreras in the postseason. Without him, they’re going to be looking far and wide for their power in the lineup.

item.content:encoded:
Adley Rutschman and his Boston Red Sox will take on the Chicago Cubs at Tropicana Field, on Sunday, Sept. 27 at 3:05 p.m. ET. Rutschman has +600 odds to hit a home run as of Sunday afternoon.
What It Means
Rutschman is hitting for a .240 BA, .312 OBP and .417 SLG with a 16.7% strikeout rate and a 9.3% walk rate. His OPS is .729 and he has scored 43 runs. In 407 plate appearances, he has hit 12 home runs and driven in 59 runs. In his most recent appearance, he racked up two hits (going 2 for 4 with two RBIs) against the Cubs.
Shota Imanaga makes the start for the Cubs, his 32nd of the season. He is 11-10 with a 3.74 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 173 1/3 innings pitched.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox Announce Surprise Decision on Starting Pitcher Before Cubs Season Finale
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Vankin
item.description: The Boston Red Sox made a surprise announcement before their season-ending game against the Chicago Cubs in Tampa Bay Sunday. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox made a surprise announcement before their season-ending game against the Chicago Cubs in Tampa Bay Sunday. Tanner Houck will take the mound for the Red Sox, starting the game and concluding an injury rehab that has stretched more than 16 months since his last big league pitch.
The assignment came together late, a sign of how unsettled Boston’s roster still is, and it puts real pressure on an arm that hasn’t thrown a competitive pitch since Tommy John surgery sidelined him last year.
Game 162 was never supposed to happen in Florida. A forecasted nor’easter pushed the finale to Tropicana Field, according to theScore‘s Simon Sharkey-Gotlieb, sending both clubs to St. Petersburg right after Friday’s doubleheader at Fenway Park.
Boston is locked into the American League’s No. 5 seed and opens the Wild Card Series Tuesday at Yankee Stadium. The Cubs, already in the playoffs, send left-hander Shota Imanaga to the mound while they play out the string for seeding.
MLB.com’s own lineup page still listed Boston’s starter as TBD deep into Sunday morning, but beat reporters closed the gap first, with The Boston Globe’s Tim Healey and MassLive’s Chris Cotillo both confirming Houck’s assignment hours before first pitch.
| BOSTON RED SOX — ROSTER MOVES | |
|---|---|
| Move | Details |
| Recalled | Infielder/outfielder Nate Eaton and right-handed pitcher Wyatt Olds. |
| Reinstated | Right-handed pitcher Tanner Houck from the 60-Day Injured List; he will start today’s game against the Chicago Cubs. |
| Placed on IL | Catcher/first baseman Mickey Gasper — 10-Day IL (retroactive to Sept. 26), right biceps strain. |
| Placed on IL | Right-handed pitcher Tyron Guerrero — 15-Day IL (retroactive to Sept. 24), right shoulder strain. |
| Transferred | Outfielder Eli White to the 60-Day Injured List. |
| Boston Red Sox roster moves, Fenway Park, Boston, MA. | |
Tanner Houck and the Boston Red Sox’s 16-Month Wait
Houck’s 2025 season came apart fast. He opened the year as Boston’s No. 2 starter behind Garrett Crochet, then posted an 8.04 ERA across nine outings, including two starts in which he allowed 11 earned runs apiece, against Tampa Bay and Detroit.
That Detroit start, a 14-2 loss in which he walked three and struck out none, stands as Houck’s last big league appearance before Sunday.
He landed on the injured list days later with a right flexor strain, and a rehab assignment that July got cut short by the same elbow. Tommy John surgery followed in August 2025, then a return to the 60-day injured list this past February wiped out his entire 2026 regular season.
Houck made his final tuneup Saturday, Sept. 19, for Triple-A Worcester, allowing two runs, one earned on a solo homer, over 3 1/3 relief innings, his fourth and last rehab outing.
“Long year, long process. But this was the goal from Day 1,” Houck said, recalling the target he set in spring, as quoted by MLB.com‘s Ian Browne.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept his read on Houck simple.
“Let’s see how these outings go and how he feels and go from there,” Tracy said, as quoted by MLB.com.

Boston Red Sox Weigh Tanner Houck for October
Houck, 30, was Boston’s first-round pick in 2017, No. 24 overall out of Missouri, debuted in September 2020 and is now the longest-tenured player on the Red Sox roster. He made the All-Star team in 2024, going 9-10 with a 3.12 ERA over 30 starts, and carries a career mark of 24-32 with a 3.97 ERA and 449 strikeouts across parts of seven seasons.
None of that guarantees him a Wild Card Series spot. According to a Just Baseball roster projection, however, Houck may beat out fellow rehabbing reliever Johan Oviedo for a bullpen job largely on the strength of his postseason experience.
The Boston Globe‘s Peter Abraham raised the same possibility last week, writing that Houck could factor into the Wild Card mix if his rehab wrapped up cleanly.
No official roster has been announced. Boston will make that call after tonight’s results, with Houck’s final piece of evidence sitting right in front of them.

item.dc:creator: Jackson Kruse
item.description: Boston Red Sox catcher Mickey Gasper exited Game 1 of Friday's doubleheader against the Chicago Cubs at Fenway Park with an apparent injury after striking out in the bottom of the fifth inning. After striking out swinging on a pitch in the dirt, Gasper walked off the field while flexing his right arm. Boston Red Sox Catcher Mickey Gasper Leaves Chicago Cubs Game With Injury: Latest Update Connor Wong replaced Gasper at catcher in the sixth inning. After Gasper's strikeout, the Red Sox tied the g
item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox
catcher Mickey Gasper exited Game 1 of Friday's doubleheader against the Chicago Cubs at Fenway Park with an apparent injury after striking out in the bottom of the fifth inning.
After striking out swinging on a pitch in the dirt, Gasper walked off the field while flexing his right arm.
Boston Red Sox Catcher Mickey Gasper Leaves Chicago Cubs Game With Injury: Latest Update
Connor Wong
replaced Gasper at catcher in the sixth inning. After Gasper's strikeout, the Red Sox tied the game on a two-run single from Adley Rutschman.
This post will be updated with the latest information on the situation.
Update: Gasper left the game with right biceps discomfort, the Red Sox revealed to reporters.
From the Boston Globe's Tim Healey on X: Mickey Gasper left the game with right biceps discomfort, the Red Sox said.
Looking at Boston Red Sox Catcher Mickey Gasper
Gasper is a 30-year-old journeyman who has been a nice surprise for Boston this year.
Amid multiple stints in the minors, Gasper has slashed .251/.357/.466 with 10 home runs and 24 RBI in 225 plate appearances across 67 games with Boston this year.
The New York Yankees selected Gasper in the 27th round (No. 817 overall) of the 2018 MLB Draft out of college.
The 27th round no longer exists in the MLB Draft.
Gasper never reached the majors with New York. The Red Sox drafted the catcher in the minor-league phase of the 2023 Rule 5 Draft.
Gapser made his MLB debut with the Red Sox, his childhood team, in 2024. He went hitless in 18 at-bats with Boston in his first MLB season.
The Minnesota Twins acquired Gasper from the Red Sox in the 2024-25 offseason. He hit just .158/.257/.232 with two home runs and 11 RBI over 45 games with Minnesota.
The Twins designated Gasper over the winter. The Washington Nationals claimed him off waivers, only to DFA him nine days later, allowing the Red Sox to require the backstop via a waiver claim.
This article was originally published on HEAVY

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Roman Anthony rakes as Red Sox take Game 1 vs. Cubs
item.dc:creator: Jake Reiser
item.description: Alec Gamboa is not a starter. At least not at the Major League level caliber. But when the Red Sox needed someone to open a doubleheader on the last Friday of the regular season, they handed it to him anyway—and the Cubs made him pay for it quickly. Tyrone Taylor doubled in the first inning to put Chicago on the board. Miguel Amaya followed with a two-run double in the second. Three runs in two innings, Clay Holmes cruising, and the Sox in a hole before most of Fenway (whoever was going to brave
item.content:encoded:
Alec Gamboa is not a starter. At least not at the Major League level caliber. But when the Red Sox needed someone to open a doubleheader on the last Friday of the regular season, they handed it to him anyway—and the Cubs made him pay for it quickly.
Tyrone Taylor doubled in the first inning to put Chicago on the board. Miguel Amaya followed with a two-run double in the second. Three runs in two innings, Clay Holmes cruising, and the Sox in a hole before most of Fenway (whoever was going to brave the risk of weather) had settled into their seats.
Then the defense took over.
Caleb Durbin threw Matt Shaw out at the plate in the second inning to keep the Cubs from stretching it further. Isiah Kiner-Falefa made a sliding grab in the third. Andruw Monasterio came up with a diving catch in the fourth. Not glamorous plays in the box score, but they kept 3-0 from turning into 5-0, and that mattered later.
Roman Anthony was (finally) doing Roman Anthony things all afternoon. He went 3-for-3 with a walk and his fingerprints are on both comeback sequences that mattered. He got things started in the third when he scored on a Dansby Swanson throwing error to make it 3-1. Stayed alive. Kept the at-bats meaningful.
It stayed there until Adley Rutschman. With two on in the fifth against Caleb Thielbar, Rutschman hit a two-run double to tie the game. That's the at-bat the rest of this recap hangs on. There's no comeback without it.
The Cubs went to Aaron Civale in the seventh. Anthony tripled to right field, then Connor Wong stepped up and hit the go-ahead double. Red Sox 4, Cubs 3.
Willson Contreras didn't play game one—his hand still won't let him swing without pain. Ceddanne Rafaela sat out too. You can file away what Boston did to Chicago's depleted lineup, but you can also file away that a team down 3-0 didn't pack it in. The seventh inning happened.
Game 2 is next. They went ahead and won the first one.
Studs
Roman Anthony — 3-for-3 with a walk. On base four times. Scored on the error in the third to keep Boston in it, tripled in the seventh to set up the go-ahead, and was just relentless all afternoon. This was his game.
Adley Rutschman — utschman's two-run double off Thielbar tied it and gave the whole thing a different shape. That's what you pay for.
Connor Wong — Go-ahead double in the seventh coming in for Mickey Gasper. Simple entry in the ledger, but a needed go-ahead run.
Dud
The first two innings — Three runs on Gamboa before anyone got comfortable. Fair amount of that is on Gamboa, fair amount is just what happens when you open with a reliever and it doesn't work. The Sox survived it. They shouldn't count on that against a full-strength playoff opponent.
The wind — How many times did the wind knock balls down today? Yes for better with potential Cubbies homers knocked down, but also it's a hamper on an already struggling offense for the Sox.
Play of the Game
Rutschman's two-run double in the fifth. Down 3-1, two runners on, Cubs holding a lead that had felt comfortable since the second inning—and Rutschman turned the whole situation. That swing is why the seventh inning got to mean something.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox take Game 1 of Cubs doubleheader, cement Wild Card seeding
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: Amid whipping winds and the gathering storm off the coast, the Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs embarked upon a doubleheader Friday afternoon. item.content:encoded:
Amid whipping winds and the gathering storm off the coast, the Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs embarked upon a doubleheader Friday afternoon.
It looked bleak for the home team early on, as the Cubs took a 3-0 lead during Red Sox rookie left-hander Alec Gamboa’s two-inning opener.
But Roman Anthony is heating up at exactly the right time. His 3 for 3 performance, with two doubles, a triple, walk and two runs carried the Red Sox to a 4-3 win in the top half of the doubleheader.
The victory cemented the Red Sox as the second American League Wild Card team, meaning they are set for a rematch of last year’s Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium, which begins Tuesday.
“Just had to find a way to win there, and find a way to just kind of play Red Sox baseball as we’ve done all year, with crazy scheduling and different things,” Anthony said.
Left fielder Tyrone Taylor gave the Cubs an instant lead in the first, with a two-out RBI double after Gamboa’s one-out walk to right-fielder Seiya Suzuki. First baseman Michael Busch and shortstop Dansby Swanson slid headfirst into home in rapid succession when catcher Miguel Amaya doubled with one out in the second for a 3-0 lead.
Southpaw Jake Bennett, a starter for all 19 games of this rookie season, replaced Gamboa in the third. Bennett’s first major league relief effort encompassed 3 2/3 scoreless innings in which he yielded three hits, walked one and struck out one.
“He looked very comfortable, and was able to get in the zone right away,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said.
“Definitely a little bit of an adrenaline rush, but at the end of the day it’s the same game,” Bennett said of the difference between starting and relieving. “Just in the case that I have to come out of the bullpen in the wild card, just good to have some experience doing it at this level.”
Righty Greg Weissert (1 1/3 IP) and lefty Raymond Burgos (2 IP) held the Cubs off the rest of the way.
The Red Sox pitching staff entered Friday with 41 games with one or zero runs allowed, not only the most in the majors this season, but the club’s most in a season since the Live-Ball Era began in 1920. The Red Sox entered Friday with the third-best ERA in MLB. If they can hang on through the rest of the weekend, it will be their first season in the top three since 2007.
The bats have been Boston’s bigger issue this month, and most of the season, by far. Through 22 September games including Game 1 on Friday, the Red Sox are averaging 7.5 runners left on base per game, matching their dismal May mark.
Yet, the Red Sox were 2 for 13 with runners in scoring position, and left eight men on base, but they outhit the Cubs, 9-7, drew four walks and only struck out four times for an improvement over recent games.
“Quite a few guys that swung the bats well, we got tons of big hits, especially in the second part of the game,” Tracy said. “It was a really good offensive showing, for sure.”
After his wasted leadoff double in the first, Anthony scored the only Red Sox run through four innings, on Swanson’s throwing error in the bottom of the third.
Anthony’s second double off Cubs starter Clay Holmes went to better use. He followed Isiah Kiner-Falefa’s leadoff single in the fifth, and both men scored when designated hitter Adley Rutschman greeted lefty reliever Caleb Thielbar with a two-run single.
Holmes, a longtime New York Yankee, went 4 1/3 innings on 78 pitches (50 strikes). He allowed three runs, two earned, on five hits, walked three and struck out three.
Red Sox catcher Mickey Gasper was Holmes’ final batter. After striking out against Holmes for the third time, Gasper was replaced at catcher by Connor Wong for the top of the sixth due to what the Red Sox later announced as right biceps discomfort.
“He’s in some pretty good discomfort,” Tracy said of Gasper, who underwent an MRI after the game.
Wong’s entry proved otherwise fortuitous in the bottom of the seventh. His 12th double of the year rocketed down the third-base line, and Anthony, who tripled, jogged home for the go-ahead run.
That Anthony used the whole field with a double to left, double to center, and triple to right was among the most encouraging aspects of his offensive showing. Particularly as the swirling winds sent balls flying in unusual directions throughout the game.
“When I’m using that other way, that’s the biggest thing for me, I’ve had a lot of success in the past, and when I’m going well, I’m hitting it where it’s pitched, and taking advantage of that wall over there, even on windy days like today,” Anthony said. “Just kind of continue to pass it along, and try to be just a problem (for pitchers) any way that you possibly can.”
It fell to Burgos to protect the one-run lead in the ninth. The Red Sox southpaw did so with a 1-2-3 inning that included winning a 10-pitch at-bat against National League MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong for the second out.
The Red Sox are 86-74, with two regular-season games left to play.
After that, they’re on to New York.

item.content:encoded:
Let’s play two!
With a nor’easter rolling into the area, the Cubs and Red Sox are looking to get ahead of the weather by playing a doubleheader Friday. The first game, with a 1:05 p.m. start, was originally Sunday’s contest. The teams will suit up again for a 5:35 p.m. first pitch in the nightcap — moved up slightly from its original 7:10 p.m. start, then again Thursday morning from a 6:05 start.
The Red Sox’ offense is still trying to find its form heading into October. Boston has lost four of five and has not scored more than two runs in any game during that stretch.
The Red Sox managed just two singles in Thursday’s 1-0 loss to the Guardians. In Wednesday’s 1-0 win, Andruw Monasterio snapped an 0-for-21 skid with an RBI single.
“Over these next three games, if you see some [offense] bust out, that would be great,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “We did have some quality plate appearances from certain guys, which was good to see.”
Willson Contreras sat out his sixth consecutive game. Contreras was hit in the right hand by a pitch a week ago, and said he couldn’t swing a bat the past two days. Tracy hopes to have Contreras back for postseason play when it begins Tuesday, but the first baseman gave a disappointing update about his condition.
“It’s really frustrating when you’re doing the best you can do, you’re expecting to heal faster and it doesn’t happen,” he said.
Alec Gamboa gets the nod for the Red Sox in the opener, followed by Brayan Bello in the second game. Gamboa, who has never faced the Cubs, owns a 0.50 ERA in his past 13 outings.
The Cubs are expected to start Clay Holmes and David Peterson — both midseason acquisitions from the Mets — in the Friday games.
Here’s a preview for this afternoon’s contest.

Game 2 Pitching: LHP David Peterson (9-8, 4.96 ERA)
RED SOX (85-74): Anthony LF, Gasper C, Rutschman DH, Abreu RF, Durbin 3B, Sogard 2B, Duran CF, Monasterio 1B, Kiner-Falefa SS
Game 1 Pitching: LHP Alec Gamboa (1-0, 1.16 ERA)
Game 2 Pitching: RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA)
Game 1 time: 1:05 p.m.
Game 2 time: 5:35 p.m.
TV, radio: NESN, WEEI-FM 93.7
Cubs vs. Gamboa: Has not faced any Cubs batters
Red Sox vs. Holmes: Wilyer Abreu 2-5, Willson Contreras 5-11, Jarren Duran 0-6, Isiah Kiner-Falefa 3-7, Ceddanne Rafaela 0-3, Adley Rutschman 2-4, Nick Sogard 0-2, Trevor Story 1-8, Connor Wong 1-3
Stat of the day: The Red Sox own a 39-39 record at home this season.
Notes: The Cubs downed the Marlins, 2-1, Thursday afternoon to secure their second straight postseason berth. ... Pete Crow-Armstrong became the seventh 40-homer, 40-steal player in major league history after stealing second base in the first inning. Crow-Armstrong, the National League MVP favorite, has 45 homers and 40 steals. ... The Cubs occupy the second NL wild-card spot. Chicago is a game behind the Padres and one game up on the Phillies. The top wild-card team hosts through the opening round of the playoffs.
Cam Kerry can be reached at cam.kerry@globe.com.

item.title: [Audacy] Why Willson Contreras' hand means so much to the Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Rob Bradford
item.description: There was the 1-0 loss to the Guardians. There were the weather updates that might very well have the Red Sox and Cubs playing somewhere other than Fenway Park this weekend. And there was Ceddanne Rafaela's return from his hamstring scare. But when it came to news that mattered for the Red Sox, it was hard to top what Willson Contreras said after this latest defeat. The first baseman's bruised right hand evidently does not seem to be cooperating when it comes to postseason readiness. "I mean, it
item.content:encoded:
There was the 1-0 loss to the Guardians. There were the weather updates that might very well have the Red Sox and Cubs playing somewhere other than Fenway Park this weekend. And there was Ceddanne Rafaela's return from his hamstring scare.
But when it came to news that mattered for the Red Sox, it was hard to top what Willson Contreras said after this latest defeat.
The first baseman's bruised right hand evidently does not seem to be cooperating when it comes to postseason readiness.
"I mean, it's really concerning,” Contreras said. “But at the same time, I'm putting all my effort -- and everything I can do, I'm doing it. I don't know what else to say. I’m working hard with the trainers; the hand is slowly getting better. But I haven’t been able to swing the last two days. I’ll be honest with the team. I know Tuesday is a really important game. It's a really important series, and I'll be completely honest with the team.”
Contreras added, "It's frustrating, if I’m being honest. I was hoping to swing today, and I couldn't swing. I came into my locker just tearing up because that's what we play for. We play to play in October, and it's really frustrating when we're doing the best you can do and you're expecting to heal faster and that doesn't happen."
It appeared as though Contreras was headed in the right direction, taking an exorbitant amount of swings prior to Tuesday's game, both on the Fenway field and underneath with the Trajekt pitching machine. But the results from the exercise were not positive, with the righty hitter unable to replicate any sort of batting practice over the last couple of days.
There is still time for Contreras, with the Red Sox's first wild-card game on Tuesday. But his original plan to use the weekend games against the Cubs as a tune-up for the playoffs seems extremely unlikely.
Why is this such a big deal? It's because of the skill-set Contreras carries, one that the Red Sox seem starved for heading into the postseason.
All good postseason runs are usually built on the back of top-of-the-order power, with opponents needing to navigate their way through a team's alpha batters. Hitting home runs, in particular, is usually a top priority. The Blue Jays and Dodgers lived that life a year ago, as did the Yankees and Los Angeles the year before. You know who didn't? The 2025 Red Sox during their three wild-card games at Yankee Stadium.
Trevor Story's solo homer in Game 2 of last season's playoff showdown with the Yankees marked the only time a Red Sox player cleared the fences. It was a deficiency that was difficult to ignore.
It was why Craig Breslow proclaimed early in the offseason that his team needed more power. It was the reason acquiring Curtis Mead became a priority heading into the trade deadline. And it is why Contreras, who leads the Red Sox with 27 homers, has been so important. (The Red Sox are 18-8 when Contreras hits at least one homer.)
While this Red Sox team has taught us that things can turn in a hurry, the way the Sox's offense has been trending isn't good. In the last five games, the Sox have hit only two home runs. And in September, Chad Tracy's team has the second-lowest batting average and OPS in baseball, while scoring the fewest runs (13 fewer than the next-worst).
There are potential solutions to the Red Sox's postseason power problem, including Roman Anthony (who is tied with Mickey Gasper for the team lead in homers for September with four), Adley Rutschman, Story, Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu, who has two home runs since Aug. 16.
But Contreras has always been the constant ... until now.
“When it hurts, it hurts. Especially when it's the top hand,” Contreras said. “If it was the bottom hand, I could swing with the right hand, but when it's the right hand, my right hand just feels weaker until I just let the bat go. It's not a good sign. ... Again, I'm doing everything that I can to come back and play with the boys and be there with the boys. But sometimes you have to listen to your body, and I'm listening to the trainers and doing everything that they ask me to do, and [it's] just one of those things that I can't control."

item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony is out of the Boston Red Sox lineup, raising an immediate question about whether something is wrong with the young star.
Here’s why Anthony is out of the lineup and what his absence means for the Red Sox.
Anthony is out of the Boston Red Sox lineup Thursday against Cleveland, but the club has not attached any new injury news to the decision.
Thursday is Anthony’s first day off since he returned from the injured list. The Red Sox have just three regular-season games left to play after Thursday.

Roman Anthony’s Lineup Status for Guardians Series Finale
Manager Chad Tracy had not yet explained the absence when the club posted the lineup ahead of his pregame media session.
The rest of the card shows how the night is built. Jarren Duran starts in left field, Mickey Gasper takes the designated hitter spot and Ceddanne Rafaela returns to center. Gasper bats right-handed, and Cleveland counters with right-hander Daniel Espino, according to MLB.com‘s lineup page. Left-hander Ranger Suarez (8-4, 3.27 ERA) starts for Boston.
Rafaela left Wednesday’s 1-0 win with right hamstring tightness and was set to undergo an MRI Thursday, according to the Boston Globe. Duran replaced Rafaela in the third inning and went 2-for-3, according to the Globe‘s recap. Willson Contreras sits again.
Gasper was among the players optioned to make room for Anthony’s return.
“It was bittersweet. Like, I really mean it,” Tracy said, as quoted by Yahoo Sports.
Boston has already clinched a playoff spot. Tuesday’s card benched Trevor Story, Duran and Contreras with no public explanation, according to NESN reporter Rodney Knuppel.

Boston Red Sox Playoff Plans for Roman Anthony
No report ties Thursday’s absence to the right ring finger that cost Anthony nearly four months. He left a May 4 game at Detroit with wrist and hand discomfort, later described as a partially torn ligament, according to NESN‘s injury timeline.
Rehab stalled. Anthony “hasn’t made any substantive progress,” Tracy said in a late-June update, as quoted by Boston.com.
The Red Sox shifted him to the 60-day list and sent him to Fort Myers. Even after 3 1/2 months, the club declined to circle a return date, according to the Boston Globe. He was finally activated on Aug. 30, according to NBC Sports.
He has hit .242/.294/.432 with four home runs in 22 games since activation. His return began 10-for-22 over five games, then cooled to .137/.214/.296 across 56 plate appearances through Sept. 18. That night at Tampa Bay he hit a 438-foot leadoff homer, according to CBS Sports. He went 0-for-5 Tuesday and 1-for-4 Wednesday, according to CBS Sports‘ game log.
Tracy has resisted singling out Anthony during cold stretches.
“It’s not a Roman thing,” he said in May, as quoted by The Boston Globe.
Anthony wants the October he missed in 2025 with an oblique injury, and he said he is “where I want to be,” as quoted by The Boston Globe. The AL wild-card series opens Tuesday.
Anthony remains active and available off the bench. Any appearance Thursday would likely come as a pinch hitter, a role for his left-handed bat late in the game.

item.title: [tsn.ca] Blue Jays finish season sitting 16th in MLB Power Rankings
item.dc:creator: ESPN
