item.content:encoded:
If you wanted an early preview of what playoff baseball will look like for the Boston Red Sox in 2026, Wednesday night was that exact setup.
The Texas Rangers are fighting for their playoff lives, while the Red Sox have the luxury of having their wild-card spot all but assured. That meant Texas threw the best pitchers they could from start to finish, with MacKenzie Gore handing off to Jakob Junis in the middle innings before ex-Red Sox Nathan Eovaldi piggybacked the final four innings.
Well, the Red Sox only had three hits on the night in a disappointing 7-3 loss, and it highlighted a larger problem. Too many of this team's key offensive contributors are sleepwalking through September, with young star outfielder Roman Anthony topping the short list. Let's break down the three primary culprits.
1. Roman Anthony
Anthony came off the injured list guns blazing at first, but the last 11 games have been a grind. He's 7-for-49 (.149 AVG) with a .429 OPS and just one extra-base hit in those last 51 plate appearances. He's not taking his walks, he's not hitting for power, and he looks caught in between on far too many swings.
Too much of this offense was built to run through Anthony, which is evident as much when he's struggling as it was when he was injured. But if Willson Contreras isn't going to homer every night, then Anthony has to be ready to provide a big swing in October. This is where it would have really helped for him to have gotten some playoff experience last year.
2. Adley Rutschman
You can be certain that when the Red Sox gave up five pieces for Rutschman , including three of their top five prospects, they expected more than a .609 OPS and 0.1 bWAR in the first 24 games. But the trade was made to have a locked-in starting catcher for October who could add thump to the lineup, so all could soon be forgiven.
Rutschman just isn't making enough quality contact, and one can almost see him pressing to make up for the slow start that was exacerbated by wrist and elbow injuries. It's easy to tell a guy he needs to find more barrels, but a lot harder to find the advice that gets him to do it.
3. Wilyer Abreu
Abreu is having one of the quietest 6-WAR seasons in recent memory, and it's not as if the Red Sox should be demanding more from him, all things considered. That said, for this team to make a deep playoff run, the notoriously streaky lefty is going to have to get hot.
While Abreu can carry a team when he's seeing the ball well, his propensity for hitless games is worth tracking. He's got five of them already in September, including the last two in a row, and while he's been better in the second half than the first, his last few games have looked shaky.
Jackson Roberts is a former Division III All-Region DH who now writes and talks about sports for a living. A Bay Area native and a graduate of Swarthmore College and the Newhouse School at Syracuse University, Jackson makes his home in North Jersey. He grew up rooting for the Red Sox, Patriots, and Warriors, and he recently added the Devils to his sports fandom mosaic. item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Red Sox's Big Advantage From Adley Rutschman Deal So Far
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: The Boston Red Sox certainly made the right call by going out and acquiring Adley Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles. Now, of course, the All-Star backstop has taken some heat for offensive struggles since joining the organization. But there is more to the game than just batting average and Rutschman has been a clear positive for the organization. Offensively, he'll get right. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox certainly made the right call by going out and acquiring Adley Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles.
Now, of course, the All-Star backstop has taken some heat for offensive struggles since joining the organization. But there is more to the game than just batting average and Rutschman has been a clear positive for the organization. Offensively, he'll get right. He has been too good throughout his big league career so far to not get back on track.
Even though he hasn't been as explosive as expected offensively, it has been overlooked just how good he has been behind the plate. His defense has been good enough to the point that it's an advantage for Boston when he is catching. He's in the 98th percentile in framing and the 96th percentile in caught stealing above average. Plus, Boston hurlers have done well, for the most part, with him behind the plate.
Even that's not all, though. An underrated area in which Rutschman has improved the Red Sox is with his ABS challenges. Rutschman is 18-for-26 (69.2 percent) on ABS challenges since joining the Red Sox, as pointed out on X by MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo.
Boston has been in the middle of the pack throughout the 2026 season when it comes to challenges. Right now, the Red Sox are 15th in the league with a 50 percent success rate (80-for-161). That's a number that has been positively impacted by the addition of Rutschman, to say the least.
Think back to earlier in the season. Boston actually really struggled with ABS challenges to the point that it was a talking point around the club. Now, Boston doesn't look like one of the worst clubs at challenging any longer. The addition of Rutschman is the biggest reason why. He's one of the best players in baseball at it. In fact, the All-Star catcher is eighth in the league in net overturns vs. expected at 14.2. Rutschman is 41-20 on the season in total across 61 challenges (67 percent).
Rutschman clearly has an elite understanding of the strike zone. This is important in itself. In comparison, former Red Sox catcher Carlos Narváez has a 53 percent success rate on challenges (42-for-79) and is -5.5 on net overturns vs. expected.
Rutschman hasn't gotten hot offensively yet, but he has done well with the Red Sox's starting rotation and has added an element behind the plate Boston hasn't had. Imagine the impact he'll have when his bat does get going?
This is why the Red Sox gave up an arm and a leg for him. He is among the elite of the elite behind the plate and fortunately, he's in Boston.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.content:encoded:
When Erik Miller on September 16 took the mound in front of the Texas Rangers, it didn't take long for things to go awry. Miller's command has never been perfect, but something was definitely off in Arlington, Texas.
It took only three pitches for the big lefty to plunk Corey Seager, and he walked Jake Burger two batters later. On his lone pitch to Brandon Nimmo, the former New York Met knocked a game-changing RBI double to center field, and things crumbled from there.
Ezequiel Duran's two-RBI single, which gave the Rangers a three-run lead, was the last at-bat of the inning before Miller was spared by Adley Rutschman catching Duran stealing. The outing was Miller's worst since he joined the Boston Red Sox at the trade deadline — he allowed three runs on two hits, a walk and a hit batter with one strikeout.
The outing against the Rangers was the second one in as many games that has given Miller trouble. On September 13 against the Kansas City Royals, Miller lasted just a third of an inning after conceding two walks and a fielder's choice. Garrett Whitlock entered after him and gave up a single, but the Royals' lone run of the game was charged to Miller.
Red Sox need Erik Miller to right recent command issues as soon as possible to be right for postseason
After his appearance in Texas, Miller made a concerning statement about his recent struggles. It could be a disastrous sign for Boston's October bullpen.
"Kinda working through some stuff right now," Miller said. "There's some stuff I'm trying to clean up a little bit on the mechanical side. I mean, at some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. I had been doing really well and there are some bad habits I'm kinda falling back into so, yeah, just gotta work through it, gotta get back to what I was doing and go from there."
Miller has been one of Boston's biggest relief weapons since the trade deadline. The Red Sox need him in his best shape all the more with Tyron Guerrero on the injured list and after the announcement that Justin Slaten's season has ended.
Before his shaky command popped up, Miller had done a solid job at limiting free passes, one of the major concerns from his tenure with the Giants. Over his 12 outings in August (including one with the Giants) Miller allowed three walks and a hit batter (0.943 WHIP). Through five outings in September, he's up to six walks and a hit batter (2.077 WHIP). The combination of fatigue and decreased command will make for a brutal outcome for Boston.
Thankfully, the Red Sox are expecting some relief reinforcements for the playoff run. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working toward returns in long relief. But having them plus prime Miller would be the best outcome.
The Red Sox must work more closely with Miller to address his mechanical issue, whatever it is. Over his last two outings, he's served up damaging pitches or free passes, and that won't get Boston far in October, especially given the fatigue its rotation has been showing.

item.title: [MLB.com] Contreras blasts off after early challenge, but Red Sox's 'pen falters late
item.dc:creator: Perla Paredes

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON -- Despite getting an early two-run homer from Willson Contreras and taking advantage of a handful of Rangers miscues, the Red Sox couldn’t hold off Texas in a 7-3 loss on Wednesday at Globe Life Field.
The loss, however, didn’t change Boston's position in the postseason race, as the club remained in the second AL Wild Card spot and maintained its five-game cushion over the White Sox after Chicago lost to the Guardians earlier Wednesday.
Roman Anthony opened the game with a four-pitch walk. After Jahmai Jones flied out, Wilyer Abreu grounded into a forceout but beat the relay throw to first to avoid the double play and keep the inning alive for Contreras.
“Those are important details,” Contreras said in Spanish. “They don’t go unnoticed because they matter a lot in this game.”
With the postseason nearing, those -- along with having success with ABS challenges -- are the types of details Contreras was glad to see the Red Sox execute, especially with close games likely to become more common down the stretch. Boston had six successful challenges Wednesday night, and catcher Adley Rutschman improved to 19-for-27 on ABS challenges since joining the Red Sox.
Contreras entered the night batting .563 in his career against Rangers starter MacKenzie Gore, and helped set up his two-run homer with an early ABS challenge on a called strike that missed the bottom of the zone. After the call was overturned, Contreras took advantage when Gore left an 87 mph slider over the middle of the plate, sending it out to left-center field for his 27th homer of the season and an early 2-0 Red Sox lead.
“Honestly, I really liked that challenge, because I was sure it was a little bit under,” Contreras said. “And after that, I had the opportunity to get a pitch a little bit higher and connect for a home run.”
Contreras’ familiarity with Gore has also helped. The two faced each other frequently when Gore was with the Nationals and Contreras played for the Cubs and Cardinals.
“I know him well and I know that he always makes one or two errors in a game, so I am always trying to be ready for that error, like today,” Contreras said. “I wasn’t looking for that pitch, I was just looking for him to miss his spot in the middle.”
It was Contreras’ 27th homer of the season and his first since Aug. 21 against the Giants.
Texas eventually erased that advantage, pulling even at 2 in the fourth, but the Rangers helped Boston regain the lead an inning later.
Caleb Durbin drew Boston’s third walk of the night against Gore to begin the fifth. Trevor Story then sent a liner toward third baseman Josh Jung, who was unable to make a play. Durbin immediately recognized the opportunity, rounding second and advancing to third as Jung was slow to get the ball back into the infield.
The sequence ended Gore’s night and brought right-hander Jakob Junis out of the Rangers' bullpen. As Junis came set to face pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper, the ball slipped out of his glove for a balk, allowing Durbin to score and put the Red Sox back in front.
“We're going through it a little bit,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “We didn't create a ton of opportunities. Obviously, Willson with a big swing to give us the lead, and only a couple other chances. ... That's it. So really, [getting] three runs on the board with only three hits was good in that sense. But just not creating a ton of opportunities for ourselves today.”
The 3-2 lead was short-lived, as Texas answered in the bottom half of the fifth to tie the game again.
Boston’s starter, Jake Bennett, worked through a 26-pitch first inning, limiting Texas to one run despite allowing two doubles and a single, before giving up another run in the fourth.
The game turned in the seventh, when reliever Erik Miller allowed three runs on two hits. Texas added another run in the eighth off Raymond Burgos.
“As a team, I think we're doing the best we can to capitalize on every chance we have,” Contreras said. “We battle. We come here with the right mindset. We work hard. We work on details that we need to get better on.
“And sometimes it doesn't matter how hard you work. Sometimes the results are not gonna come. But you have to build off that. You have to take those types of games personal and get better for tomorrow.”

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox held to three hits, drop series to Rangers with lifeless loss
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr

item.content:encoded:
The limp to October goes on for the Boston Red Sox, who blew an early 2-0 lead Wednesday night, and dropped the series in Texas with a 7-3 loss that improved the Rangers to 76-76.
Boston batters managed just three hits, their runs coming via Willson Contreras’ first-inning two-run homer and Caleb Durbin scoring on a balk in the fifth.
Early on, it looked like both starting pitchers were not going to last long.
Rangers lefty MacKenzie Gore began Wednesday’s game with a four-pitch walk, three of which were nowhere near the zone, to Red Sox leadoff man Roman Anthony, and gave up Contreras’ team-leading 27th homer.
Sox rookie southpaw Jake Bennett labored through a 26-pitch bottom of the first in which he faced six batters and gave up a run.
But after a second-inning delay in which it seemed like Gore was about to depart, he completed four innings. Bennett went 4 2/3. Both starters allowed three earned runs, though Gore only yielded two hits to Bennett’s eight.
“Overall, not horrible,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters of Bennett. “The first inning they were able to make him throw some pitches, so the pitches stacked up on him. But at the end of the day, he left with the lead, was competitive. … Usually you’re accustomed to see him pitching deeper, but they were pesky with their at-bats, fouled a lot of stuff off, and drove the count up.”
The Red Sox retook the lead on Jakob Junis’ fifth-inning balk. It evaporated for good one pitch into Greg Weissert’s appearance when he took over for Bennett in the bottom of the inning.
Erik Miller’s three-run blowup seventh inning was the unnecessary coup de grâce for a Red Sox team struggling to so much as collect a hit, much less score a run. But it marked Miller’s worst outing of the season, with Boston or San Francisco, and his third time allowing runs in his last six appearances.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well, just not getting ahead of guys, falling behind counts, getting into hitters counts,” a subdued Miller told reporters postgame. “I mean, doesn’t really matter how good your stuff is; guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end as well.”
“Just kind of working through some stuff right now,” Miller continued. “There’s some stuff (I’m) trying to clean up a little bit on the mechanical side. … At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. And I’d been doing really well, and some bad habits kind of fallen back into. So yeah, just got to work through it, kind of get back to what I was doing, and go from there.”
2018 World Series hero Nathan Eovaldi closed out the win with four shutout innings against his former team. It marked the veteran righty’s first relief appearance since 2020: Game 4 of the 2021 ALCS with the Red Sox.
To add insult to the injury of Boston’s decision not to re-sign Eovaldi following the 2022 season, his 46 wins since 2023 are tied for second-most among all American League pitchers in that span.
Trevor Story’s infield single in the fifth and Nick Sogard’s pinch-hit single in the sixth comprised the rest of Boston’s hits. The lineup managed three walks and struck out three times in the contest. They were 0 for 7 with runners in scoring position, and left three men on base.
“Yeah, we’re going through it a little bit,” Tracy said of his lineup. “We didn’t have a ton, we didn’t create a ton of opportunities.”
Game highlights were few and far between for the Red Sox. The short list included the usual elite defense from right fielder Wilyer Abreu, who is all but guaranteed to win his third consecutive Gold Glove Award, and continued displays of ABS expertise by new catcher Adley Rutschman, who went 3 for 3 in challenges.
The Red Sox have lost five of their last seven games since their five-game win streak. They are 7-7 in September, 10-11 in their last 20 games, and 82-70 overall.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason spot is five. But there is little magic lately.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Announce Jarren Duran Lineup Decision Before Rangers Game
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Vankin
item.description: The Boston Red are losers of four games out of their last six after dropping Tuesday's 4-2 decision to the Texas Rangers. As they push to clinch a playoff spot, the Red Sox send rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69, 83 K) to the mound in the middle contest of the three game series in Texas. Duran is sitting out again Wednesday as the Boston Red Sox face Texas Rangers left-hander
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red are losers of four games out of their last six after dropping Tuesday's 4-2 decision to the Texas Rangers.
As they push to clinch a playoff spot, the Red Sox send rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69, 83 K) to the mound in the middle contest of the three game series in Texas.
Just hours before first pitch, the Red Sox announced a decision on their left-swinging outfielder Jarren Duran.
Duran is sitting out again Wednesday as the Boston Red Sox face Texas Rangers left-hander MacKenzie Gore, extending a pattern now seven starts deep. The decision appears to be strictly a platoon move by interim manager Chad Tracy. There have been no reports that Duran is injured.
In fact, Boston has now benched its left-handed-hitting outfielder against every left-handed starter he has faced since Aug. 8, a stretch that raises concerns about how Duran fits into next season's outfield picture, and for the likely American League wild-card series matchup.
In that three-game series, the Red Sox appear certain to face at least one left-hander, possibly two, in Yankees starters Max Fried and Carlos Rodón.

| SP: Jake Bennett (LHP) • 9-7, 3.69 ERA | | | | |
| September 16, 2026 • Globe Life Field, Arlington, TX • 8:05 PM ET • Red Sox at Rangers | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | SLG |
| 1 | Roman Anthony | LF | .240 | .371 |
| 2 | Jahmai Jones | DH | .214 | .379 |
| 3 | Wilyer Abreu | RF | .255 | .463 |
| 4 | Willson Contreras | 1B | .275 | .514 |
| 5 | Adley Rutschman | C | .236 | .418 |

| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / SLG). Umpire: Nick Mahrley • Weather: 97°, Wind 9 mph • O/U: 8 Runs • Line: BOS -112 / TEX -108. | | | | |
Jarren Duran's Platoon Pattern Against Lefties
Duran bats left-handed, Gore throws left-handed, and Boston's coaching staff has ceased to start Duran on days a southpaw takes the mound for the opponent.
Nate Eaton takes over in center field for Boston.
Texas had already turned in its own lineup behind Gore hours before first pitch, setting up the Wednesday matchup at Globe Life Field.
Duran's absence from the lineup against lefties has stretched to seven straight starts without facing a southpaw, dating back to his last look at left-handed pitching on Aug. 8, according to RotoWire. He sat again Sunday against Kansas City and was used only as a pinch-hitter, a role he has filled repeatedly this month.
There is no reported health issue behind Tracy's decision. Duran started Tuesday against right-hander Jacob deGrom, playing center field and batting seventh, and remains fully active on Boston's roster.
Duran is slashing .204/.261/.361 with 20 home runs across 141 games this season, and his OPS against left-handed pitching sits at .641, actually higher than his .616 mark against right-handers, according to FanGraphs. Boston has kept sitting him against lefties anyway.
| TEXAS RANGERS STARTING LINEUP | | | | |
| SP: MacKenzie Gore (LHP) • 8-11, 4.62 ERA | | | | |
| September 16, 2026 • Globe Life Field, Arlington, TX • 8:05 PM ET • Red Sox at Rangers | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | SLG |
| 1 | Justin Foscue | 2B | .268 | .493 |
| 2 | Corey Seager | SS | .234 | .438 |
| 3 | Josh Jung | 3B | .294 | .436 |
| 4 | Jake Burger | 1B | .232 | .424 |
| 5 | Brandon Nimmo | RF | .263 | .413 |
| 6 | Wyatt Langford | LF | .239 | .435 |
| 7 | Ezequiel Duran | CF | .271 | .441 |
| 8 | Elias Díaz | DH | .239 | .405 |
| 9 | Danny Jansen | C | .192 | .359 |
| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / SLG). Umpire: Nick Mahrley • Weather: 97°, Wind 9 mph • O/U: 8 Runs • Line: BOS -112 / TEX -108. | | | | |
Duran's Playing Time Has Dropped Sharply
Duran appeared in 160 games in 2024, when he led the American League in at-bats, doubles and triples, on his way to an All-Star selection and an eighth-place MVP finish. He followed that with 157 games in 2025.
This year he has played in 141 of Boston's games, a drop that traces to the growing run of benchings against left-handed hurlers. Wednesday marks at least the seventh time this season Boston has parked Duran for a left-handed starter, following earlier sit-downs against Rodón, Kyle Freeland, Jacob Lopez, Mitch Bratt and Reid Detmers, according to CBS Sports.
Boston opened the year with four outfielders competing for time, but an early injury to Roman Anthony briefly opened the picture before Duran struggled through a rough first half, batting .194 over his first 87 games. The Duran platoon has held even as the outfield picture has grown thinner. Ceddanne Rafaela remains out with a quad injury and Eli White is sidelined with a foot issue, leaving Eaton as the only regular right-handed option in center on days Duran sits.
With the Red Sox pushing for playoff position down the stretch, Duran's shrinking role against left-handed pitching will keep drawing scrutiny. Entering Wednesday's game, the Red Sox magic number for clinching a playoff berth is five — meaning that any combination of Red Sox wins and Chicago White Sox losses totaling five puts Boston in the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Sit Jarren Duran, Shake Up Lineup For Rangers Matchup originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox will give their lineup a significantly different look Wednesday night as they attempt to respond to a frustrating series-opening loss. Jarren Duran is out of the starting lineup against Texas Rangers left-hander MacKenzie Gore. Mickey Gasper and Nick Sogard also will begin the game on the bench after starting Tuesday's 4-2 defeat at Globe Life Field.
Jahmai Jones will replace Gasper at designated hitter and bat second. Isiah Kiner-Falefa enters at second base, while Nate Eaton will take over for Duran in center field.
Boston officially announced its revamped batting order on X before the second game of the three-game series. Roman Anthony remains in the leadoff spot and will play left field. Wilyer Abreu moves from fifth to third, while Willson Contreras stays in the cleanup spot.
Adley Rutschman drops two places in the order after batting third Tuesday. The catcher will hit fifth, followed by Caleb Durbin, Trevor Story, Kiner-Falefa and Eaton.
Red Sox Lineup Vs. Rangers
- Roman Anthony, LF
- Jahmai Jones, DH
- Wilyer Abreu, RF
- Willson Contreras, 1B
- Adley Rutschman, C
- Caleb Durbin, 3B
- Trevor Story, SS
- Isiah Kiner-Falefa, 2B
- Nate Eaton, CF
Jake Bennett will start on the mound for Boston. The left-hander enters Wednesday with a 9-7 record, a 3.69 ERA and 83 strikeouts. Gore will oppose Bennett for Texas. The Rangers left-hander is 8-11 with a 4.62 ERA and 172 strikeouts.
The matchup with Gore likely contributed to manager Chad Tracy loading the bottom half of his lineup with right-handed hitters. Jones, Contreras, Durbin, Story, Kiner-Falefa and Eaton all will bat from the right side. Boston needs a better collective offensive performance after producing only two runs in Tuesday's opener. Sogard supplied both with a two-run home run against Jacob deGrom in the third inning, but the Red Sox could not complete the comeback after falling behind 4-0.
The loss dropped Boston to 82-69 with only 11 regular-season games remaining. The Red Sox entered Wednesday 9 1/2 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East and 5 1/2 games behind the New York Yankees.
Wednesday's first pitch is scheduled for 8:05 p.m. ET at Globe Life Field. NESN will carry the game.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] What Red Sox Are Expected to Do With Chad Tracy, Craig Breslow
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
Back in April, the Boston Red Sox's season was going off the rails.
The Red Sox started the season off with a 10-17 record and opted to fire a World Series-winning manager in Alex Cora — plus a handful of other coaches — and take a gamble by turning the reins over to interim manager Chad Tracy. At the time, it seemed like the sky was falling. That's because the losses kept piling up, so much so that the Red Sox were 14 games below .500 at 32-46 on June 25.
At the time, the season looked like a disaster. The Red Sox were trending towards being sellers ahead of the trade deadline, both Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet were on the Injured List with no end in sight, and it seemed like chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's seat was getting hotter and hotter. But the Red Sox transformed their season and now, with the season winding down, ESPN's Buster Olney reported on Wednesday that the expectation is that both Breslow and Tracy will stay on with Boston beyond the 2026 season.
"But Breslow's vision of a team succeeding with pitching and defense fully manifested, and the Red Sox are closing in on a playoff berth and will likely face the Yankees in the wild-card round, again," Olney wrote. "Manager Chad Tracy has been working under an interim tag all season, something of a head-scratcher; it may be that the two sides talked about the idea of an extension in midseason but set aside the topic for the offseason. But Boston is now expected to retain both Breslow and Tracy."
The Red Sox Are Making The Right Call
This is undoubtedly the right call for the Red Sox at this time.
Let's start with Breslow. Whether you love him or not, he has built a team that can go on a run. Sure, there have been some misses over the last few years. Losing Alex Bregman was a public relations disaster. Not landing one of the big free agent bats, including Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso, this past offseason also was a surprise. But there are far more wins under Breslow's belt, than losses.
Sonny Gray is going to get Cy Young Award votes and has been Boston's ace this season. Ranger Suárez was an All-Star. Willson Contreras was an All-Star. Caleb Durbin is the heart and the soul of the 2026 Red Sox. Now, the Red Sox have an All-Star catcher on their hands in Adley Rutschman. Bringing back Mickey Gasper has turned into a game-changing move. And the list goes on. The Red Sox have a roster that can make noise.
On the Tracy front, there was obviously a learning curve to being a big league manager taking over during a season, especially in such a high-profile market, like Boston. He has handled the role with grace and has clearly gotten better as the year has gone on. Plus, it doesn't hurt that the Red Sox went on a historic 15-game winning streak and put together one of the best mid-season turnarounds in MLB history. All in all, these two should both be back in 2026 and it sounds like that will be the reality.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [Field Level Media] Ranger Suarez, Red Sox snap losing streak at Royals' expense
item.description: Ranger Suarez tossed his second straight seven-inning start and the Boston Red Sox scored in their final three at-bats en route to a 5-1 win over the visiting Kansas City Royals on Saturday afternoon. Suarez (7-4) struck out eight, scattered five hits and allowed one run while completing his seven frames in 96 pitches as Boston (81-68) snapped its three-game losing streak. item.content:encoded:
Ranger Suarez tossed his second straight seven-inning start and the Boston Red Sox scored in their final three at-bats en route to a 5-1 win over the visiting Kansas City Royals on Saturday afternoon.
Suarez (7-4) struck out eight, scattered five hits and allowed one run while completing his seven frames in 96 pitches as Boston (81-68) snapped its three-game losing streak.
Roman Anthony, Adley Rutschman and Nick Sogard each had multiple hits while Wilyer Abreu hit a two-run double that gave the Red Sox a sixth-inning lead they would not relinquish.
Carter Jensen’s 24th home run of the season marked the only scoring for Kansas City (66-83), which opened the series with a win Friday.
The Red Sox took the lead with two runs on three straight hits in the sixth. After Mickey Gasper and Rutschman knocked back-to-back singles to right to chase Royals starter Randy Dobnak (3-4), Abreu drove them home with a two-out double to deep center off reliever Anthony Gose.
The lead grew in each of the next two frames, beginning with Sogard hitting a leadoff double and scoring on Caleb Durbin’s RBI single off the Green Monster in the seventh.
After Garrett Whitlock struck out the side in the Royals’ eighth, Trevor Story and Sogard posted back-to-back doubles to plate another run.
Aroldis Chapman followed with a scoreless ninth to tab Suarez with the victory.
The teams plowed through three scoreless innings with just one baserunner: Bobby Witt Jr.’s one-out single in Kansas City’s opening frame. Suarez stranded him on third after recording back-to-back outs, including an inning-ending strikeout of Vinnie Pasquantino.
Suarez retired the Royals 1-2-3 on 10 pitches in the second and third innings while Dobnak faced the minimum, striking out three batters through the first third of the game.
In the fourth, Anthony turned a leadoff single through the right side into the opening run. After moving to second on Gasper’s grounder, Anthony scored when Rutschman knocked a single into center.
After finishing the fourth around Pasquantino’s two-out double, Suarez retired five straight before Jensen’s one-out solo homer inside Pesky’s Pole in the sixth. The southpaw stranded runners in the next two frames, including back-to-back strikeouts to cap the seventh.
–Field Level Media

item.title: [Boston Herald] Patrick Sandoval allows four runs in second, Red Sox lose opener to Rangers
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second. item.content:encoded:
Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Deep down, Garrett Whitlock doesn’t think his career as a starting pitcher is over - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: Now is not the time, of course, what with the Red Sox in a playoff push and all. item.content:encoded:
Now is not the time, of course, what with the Red Sox in a playoff push and all.
But deep down inside, in a maybe-one-day-eventually sort of way, Garrett Whitlock harbors aspirations to try again to be a starting pitcher, to return to the rotation.
Consider it a curiosity.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like, ‘Hey, I’m starting.’ So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
Whitlock is intrigued enough to have picked the brain in recent months of Griffin Jax, the righthander whom the Rays converted from reliever to starter this season.
Jax, 31, had an 8.00 ERA in 11 relief appearances, moved to the rotation in April, slowly built up his pitch count, and has a 3.59 ERA in 20 starts.
Whitlock and Jax became buddies when they played together for Team USA during the World Baseball Classic in March. They’ve texted about what amounts to an experiment for Jax.
Jax’s take, per Whitlock: Everything he learned in his years as a reliever, several as a high-end reliever, made him a better pitcher, regardless of role. Tweaks to his repertoire, knowing how to attack hitters, and ensuring his body recovers between outings — it all applies to being a starter.
Whitlock has had similar conversations with the Cubs’ Clay Holmes, another Team USA teammate. He made the switch last year.
“We all joke that we’re all failed starters,” Whitlock said of his bullpen brethren.
Take it from the Royals’ Seth Lugo, who beat the Red Sox on Friday.
He and Whitlock have had very similar career arcs: They reached the majors in their mid-20s as non-elite prospects, bounced between the bullpen and rotation based on team need and their performance, and accepted their club wanting them in a relief role. They were excellent at it.
All along, Lugo, a consummate pro and good employee in his years as a Mets reliever, said he wanted to give starting another go — someday. Now, he is in his fourth season and third contract since getting the chance — once he became a free agent — and turning it into a successful and lucrative second act.
“It’s not as daunting as it seems,” Lugo said at Fenway Park over the weekend. “What happens is you first get to the big leagues and you try to be someone that you’re not, just from other influences, other recommendations. But you [learn] how to get guys out [as a reliever].
“Once you make the switch back, you have the confidence. The problems you had earlier in your career, [which] sent you to the ’pen in the first place — you’re aware why those mistakes happened.”
Lugo, like Whitlock, was a late-innings arm. He faced the other team’s best hitters in some of the most important moments of the game.
“Once you have success pitching the seventh, eighth, ninth inning, the first six innings become a lot easier,” he said. “As a reliever, when you’re going into a game, you’re a lot more stressed out than you are as a starter. So you start to recognize what you’re good at, how you can get out of those situations.”
Whitlock, who possesses a 1.81 ERA in 51 relief appearances this year, last made more than a handful of starts in 2023. Since then, he ditched the four-seam fastball to lean even more on his sinker, went with a slider instead of a sweeper, and changed his changeup, which has become highly effective.
In discussing the possibility, Whitlock is a realist: The Sox’ rotation seems full for the foreseeable future.
His contract includes team options for 2027 ($8.25 million) and 2028 ($10.5 million). Those are good deals for an elite reliever — and a really good deal for even a serviceable starter.
“I doubt Boston will do it. We’re pretty good on starting depth,” Whitlock said. “If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I’m open to it and see how it goes.”
Perez on Abreu
Royals icon and Venezuela captain Salvador Perez, witness to Wilyer Abreu’s WBC star turn, is a big fan — and a big believer of Abreu on a big stage. “He’s going to be the MVP if Boston makes it to the World Series,” Perez said. “He’s built for a moment like that.” … Early returns on Adley Rutschman’s cortisone shot last week, intended to alleviate pain in his right elbow, are solid. Against Kansas City, he went 3 for 10 with a double, as many walks as strikeouts (two) — and played three games in a row for the first time since getting hurt. “It definitely helped a lot,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “You can tell his body language and stuff too, he looks and feels pretty good.” … Garrett Crochet’s bullpen session Tuesday is scheduled for 30 pitches across two simulated innings, a step up from previous shorter sessions.
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.content:encoded:
We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.
